That apartment, when the temporary doors which divide it are thrown open, is 123 feet <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>, 30 wide, and 30 high, with an arched ceiling. It is used for public dinners, at which more than 400 persons can be commodiously seated, and also for public meetings. This room was nearly destroyed by an accidental fire in 1836, but has been restored and further beautified. One part of the building is appropriated to magisterial business, and another is occupied as a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>-office, and for the residence of the mayor's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a>-at-mace. Underneath the Exchange there are a few shops in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, but the principal part of the ground-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> is appropriated to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHAMBLES">shambles</a>. In another part of the market-place is the Subscription Library, containing more than 13,500 volumes, many of them of great value. With this is incorporated the Standfast Library, consisting of works chiefly classical and theological; making a total of nearly 15,000 volumes. There are also maps, and portraits of eminent individuals connected with the town, amongst whom are Colonel Hutchinson, Lord Byron, Sir Richard Arkwrights, Kirke White, and others. The other civic buildings are the county jail and hall, a commodious but not elegant structure; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of correction and town jail, standing on the site of a convent of the hospitalers of St John of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; the town-hall, where the borough assizes and sessions, and the mayor's and sheriff's courts are held; the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POST_OFFICE"><a class="x</a>ref" href="vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>-office, occupying a very commanding situation; and the free <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school, in which 80 boys are educated—40 in the classical, and 40 in the English department. The edifices for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship are in about the same proportion to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the inhabitants as is seen in other places which have increased with similar rapidity. St <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s is usually denominated the mother <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the town, from its priority of erection. It resembles a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> more than a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> church in its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, and its decorations, and is the most striking object in the place when viewed from what is called the High Pavement. It stands on an elevated spot, and is said to be nearly 70 feet above the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the meadows near the town. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the erection is unknown, but is said to have been in the fifteenth century. It is in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, and has a handsome square tower, in which there is a musical peal of ten bells. The length of the structure in the inside is 216 feet, the breadth at the transept 97, at the west end or principal entrance 67, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> 29 feet. The height of the tower is 126 feet, and that of the side aisles 60 feet. The porch on the south side is a very <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and elaborate piece of workmanship, which <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> has assigned to the neighbouring priory of Lenton as its original site. In the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> transept there is an excellent organ of great power. There are in this church many monumental <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> on tombs of the family of the Earls of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>, and one of an Earl of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEATH">Meath</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a> of the family of the Wrights. In the year 1848 the building, having undergone extensive repairs and numerous alterations, with a view to carrying out its original <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, was re-opened for public worship. The cost, upwards of £9,000, was defrayed by a subscription. Besides the mother church, there are provided for the adherents of the established worship the following edifices:—St <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s, St Nicholas', St James's, St Paul's, Trinity, St John Baptist's, St Matthew's, and St Mark's. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> possess a cathedral dedicated to St Barnabas, and erected in 1844 at a cost of £20,000. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NONCONFORMISTS">Nonconformists</a> have numerous places of worship, some of them large and costly. Wesley and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a> Place chapels, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> accommodate each 1800 persons, and the former is stated to have cost £10,000. Other descriptions of Methodists have 5 places of worship; the Baptists of various orders 7; the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">Independents</a> 4; the Unitarians, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, Irvingites, and numerous other sects, 1 each. In 1851 the total number of places of worship was reported as 37, of which 8 belonged to the Church of England, and 29 to other religious bodies. The largest reported attendance (on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 31) in that year was, at the several churches, 5570, and at the other places of worship 11,284. The charitable institutions depending on endowed foundations or on voluntary contributions are numerous. The Blue-Coat School clothes and educates about 50 boys and 20 girls. The General Hospital, built in 1781, possesses about two acres of land, given partly by the Duke of Newcastle and partly by the corporation. It is supported chiefly by subscriptions, and usually contains about 140 patients; whilst between 1100 and 1200 are out-patients receiving medical advice and assistance. The Dispensary, established in 1831, has on an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> 350 patients. The General Lunatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ASYLUM">Asylum</a> is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> and spacious brick building, erected in 1810, at an expense of nearly £20,000. There are extensive courts, gardens, and places for recreation; and the whole economy of the place is well contrived for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of the inmates. The foundation of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> asylum for patients of the middle class was laid by the Duke of Newcastle, October 30, 1857. Labray's and Lambley's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">Hospitals</a> are small asylums for aged widows; and Collins' Hospital is a splendid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, founded by one of the Smith family of the town, of which Lord Carrington is the present head. It consists of twenty-four small but convenient dwellings for as many <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> widows, each of whom receives four shillings weekly, and two tons and a half of coal every year. From the same endowment Carrington Street Hospital, which accommodates 20 inmates, was built between the years 1831 and 1834. Plumptre Hospital, founded by a family of that name (since transplanted into <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>) in the year 1892, but twice repaired since,—viz., in 1650 and 1751,—has been rebuilt under an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of Parliament passed in 1823. Thirteen aged widows are provided with comfortable dwellings within the house, and allowed six shillings weekly, whilst thirty others, called out-pensioners, receive ten pounds a year. Willoughby's Hospital contains nineteen tenements, the inhabitants of which receive a small pension. Woolley's Alms are dwellings for six poor persons; and Bilby's Almshouses for eight persons, who have each a loaf weekly, and two tons of coal at Christmas. Warser Gate Hospital gives apartments to six, and Hanley's to twelve poor persons. Other almshouses exist so that in the year 1844 the number of persons thus provided for was 180. In 1852 Mr George Gill erected six additional tenements for decayed workmen. Among the public edifices that deserve notice may be mentioned the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>, built in 1792, a plain building, with apartments for officers and privates, and suitable stabling for three troops of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. At the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of 1857 the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> resolved on erecting new barracks on a different site, granted by the corporation. There is an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>-room, as well as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> of moderate dimensions, and the usual provision of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAS">gas</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> works, &c. Among the comparatively recent buildings of a public character are a savings-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a>; a mechanic's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, with a hall capable of accommodating 1000 persons, a library of 6000 volumes, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-READING">reading</a>-rooms, &c.; the Artizan's Library, containing 2000 volumes; the People's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, founded by Mr George Gill in 1847, intended to bring the higher advantages of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> within <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> reach; a large and handsome asylum for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>; a ragged school; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> refuge; and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> and wash-houses. Two of the older mansions of the town are now occupied, the one as a government school of design, and the other as a people's hall, a gift to the working-classes by a benefactor whom we have already named, Mr George Gill. To these must be added a large and handsome building, erected in 1853 as a corn market, and now used as a general exchange and news-room. To this is attached a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TELEGRAPH">telegraph</a> office. The most important event in the modern history of Nottingham was the passing, on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 30, 1845, of an act for the inclosure of about 1300 acres of pasture land, by which the town was nearly encircled, and which was subject to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of common. Surrounded by this belt of open country, the town had been hemmed in upon a space of 265 acres, and was one of the most densely peopled in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>,—an immense surplus both of trade and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, properly identified with Nottingham, being located in large manufacturing villages in the immediate vicinity. The effects of the act are strikingly apparent. Many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of houses, with numerous factories, now spread over the recently-inclosed space. It is traversed by public and private <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> of more than 18 miles in length. Upwards of 50 acres are laid out, for the purposes of public recreation, in a cricket-ground, ornamental walks, and an arboretum of about 20 acres, to which there is free admission. An extensive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>-ground is included in the space reserved for public accommodation. The inclosure act also provided for the appropriation of 8 acres for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a>. Of these, four, designed for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of dissenters, were added to the general cemetery, established in 1837, and now comprising 18 acres; and the remainder are incorporated with a recently formed Church of England cemetery, containing in all 13 acres. The change in the town itself is as great as that which marks its immediate vicinity. Factories and warehouses have sprung up with a rapidity of which scarcely any other town presents an example. Almost all the leading merchants' and manufacturers have enlarged or rebuilt the places in which they carry on their business; so that Nottingham appears like a place which has suddenly become the seat of some new and very flourishing trade. The old warehouses, &c., were of the plainest character, and utterly destitute of architectural pretensions. The reverse may be said of the new. Under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Mr Hine and other able architects, the town has now been ornamented with a large number of commercial buildings, which for their architectural character will bear <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with the higher class of civic edifices to be found elsewhere. The population of Nottingham amounted in 1811 to 34,253; in 1831 it was 50,680; and in 1841, 53,091. It had grown in 1851 to 58,529, exclusive of the suburbs of Sneinton and Radford, which are now strictly incorporated with Nottingham, and constitute one town. Of these, the former contained at the last census 8840 inhabitants, and the latter 12,637; making a total of 80,006. To these ought perhaps to be added the immediately contiguous parish of Lenton, having a population of 5589. On this estimate, the population of Nottingham, taking into account its rapid increase during the last few years, cannot <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> far short of 100,000. The villages within 4 miles, and most of them, strictly speaking, dependencies of the town, contain an additional population of 30,000. The Trent is navigable up to the town; and the various <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> which branch from that river afford the means of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with every part of the kingdom. There are two distinct <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of railway connecting Nottingham with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, as well as with the north, besides lines running to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, Newark, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a>, Ilkeston, and other places. We are enabled, on the authority of W. Felkin, Esq., F.L.S., to present the following account of the two principal branches of the trade of this important town: The surprising <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a>-frame by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEE">Lee</a> has been used in one of the most interesting chapters in the history of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> invention and manufacturing industry. It was upon this machine that, about a century ago, a coarse <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of cotton <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LACE">lace</a> was first produced. The fabric was made out of one continuous thread. A beautiful adaptation of the machinery enabled a lady to make lace by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, employing for this purpose 1500 frames in Nottingham and its vicinity. This fabrication has long since died out. Then the machine was so arranged as that the material should be used altogether as warp. This very ingenious machine is still usefully and extensively employed. Mr John Heathcoat, then a working-frame smith in Nottingham, invented the bobbin-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NET">net</a> machine, and patented it in 1809. His first <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> were from 18 to 36 inches in width. A woman making lace on a pillow may produce three to five meshes or interstices in a minute. The first machine produced 1000 meshes per minute. A square yard of the produce was sold for £5. This machine, as originally constructed, though displaying wonderful mechanical skill, was a complicated one. During the whole of the intervening time incessant and remarkable ingenuity has been shown in simplifying and improving the machine. It is now made 180 to 200 inches in width; and plain net of like <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to that first made is sold currently at £6. for the square yard. A <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> turns off with easily 60,000 meshes per minute from this improved and improved by the bobbin-net machine was originally called by its talented inventor. Luddites having taken the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>'s machinery at Loughborough, he established himself at Tiverton, where he now employs 300 machines. He has represented that borough in Parliament since 1831. There are also about 100 machines at Barnstaple, 250 at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARD">Chard</a>, 100 in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Wight, and 300 in <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>. There are 2350 bobbin-net and 800 warp machines at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> in Nottingham and its vicinity. Excepting less than one-tenth of the production, the whole of the English bobbin-net machinery is employed for the Nottingham lace trade. The capital in this machinery amounts to £1,500,000, independently of that employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of doubling and throwing raw materials used in this branch of business. The number of persons wholly or in part engaged in it is 135,000, or more—as smiths, machine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, menders, warehouse men and women, finishers, embroiderers, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAGES">Wages</a> may be stated at—men 20s. to £5; youths, of both sexes, 8s. to 20s.; children, 3s. to 8s. per <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. The whole machinery, or part of it, is worked by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> or water power, where employed, upon plain or common fancy goods. The Jaccard <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> has been applied at great cost, but with perfect success, to about 2500 of the machines, making every class of bobbin-net and warp goods, up to the most expensive and close imitation of pillow <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STATISTICS">statistics</a> for 1857 may be stated, with pretty close approximation to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, as follows— Nottingham has been celebrated for its ale, the qualities of which have been the theme of song. It is still good, and very potent. Its excellence has been attributed by some to the good quality of the barley grown in the neighbourhood, by others to the purity of the water, and by many to the excellent cellars scooped out of the rock, with which most of the good houses are furnished. This town returns two members to the House of Commons. The freemen, who were formerly the sole electors, are still numerous, but are exceeded in number by the ten-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POUND">pound</a> voters. By the municipal corporation reform law passed in 1835, the town is to continue a corporation, is divided into <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> wards, and has a mayor, fourteen aldermen, and forty-two councillors, with twelve justices of the peace appointed by the crown.

NOTTINGHAMSHIRE

Pages 347-348

an inland <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, bounded on the N. by <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> and a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, on the E. by Lincolnshire, on the S. by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, and on the W. by <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>. It is of an oval <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, with its narrowest end towards the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. Its greatest length is about 50 miles, and its greatest breadth 27. Its circumference is estimated at 140 miles. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles is 822, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> 526,076 acres. The county is divided into six <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, or, as they are usually denominated, wapentakes; three of which are to the north and three to the south of the River <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>. It contains <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 207 parishes. The annual value of the real <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> assessed to the property and income tax for the year ending 5th April 1851 was £1,198,843. The number of inhabitants amounted in 1801 to 140,350; in 1811 to 162,000; in 1821 to 186,873; in 1831 to 225,400; in 1841 to 249,910; and in 1851 to 270,427. The number of inhabited houses in 1851 was 55,019. We are not enabled to state the exact proportions of the several classes engaged at that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> in trade, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, &c. According to the census of 1851, the county contains 231 public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, 58 of which are supported by endowments, and 136 by the voluntary subscriptions of members of the Established <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>. The total number of scholars in public and private day-schools is 31,178. The number of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> schools is 428, of which 183 belong to the Established Church, and 245 to other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> communions. The total number of scholars in the former is stated to be 17,785, and in the latter 26,153. The places of worship belonging to the Church of England are returned as being 248, and those belonging to other religious bodies as 382, of which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> proportion of 273 is assigned to the Wesleyan <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>. The number of sittings is reported as 160,234, of which the Established Church furnishes 76,960. The towns and villages containing more than 2000 inhabitants, and the numbers in each, were in 1851: | Town | <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> | |-----------------------|------------| | <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a> | 58,529 | | Southwell | 3,516 | | Newark | 11,330 | | Beeston | 3,016 | | <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a> | 10,627 | | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUCKNALL_TORKARD">Hucknall-Torkard</a> | 2,970 | | Basford (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>) | 10,600 | | Retford | 2,943 | | <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WORKSOP">Worksop</a> | 7,215 | | Clarborough | 2,904 | | Kirkleatham | 5,542 | | Ashfield | 2,863 | | Lenton (parish) | 5,585 | | Carlton | 2,329 | | Greasley (parish) | 5,284 | | Ruddington | 2,181 | | Arnold | 4,704 | | Blagdon | 2,054 | | Balwell | 3,786 | The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is generally <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, with moderate undulations; and its beauties are of a mild <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, somewhat picturesque in the vicinity of Sherwood Forest, but displaying neither the striking features of the adjoining county of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a> on its western side, nor the flat insipidity of the plains of Lincolnshire on its eastern side. From its position between these two descriptions of country, and from its moderate elevation, it enjoys a milder <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> than either, partaking neither of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> of the one nor the moist <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> of the other. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> temperature of the county town is said to be only 1½ below that of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, or 49°73. The dryness of the climate is favourable to early vegetation, and is supposed to be the cause of the seed-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> in Nottinghamshire commencing at the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> as in the more southern counties. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of this county is very various. On the borders of Derbyshire there is a stripe of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> with coal and <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, partly in wood, but mostly under arable culture. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">Parallel</a> to it is a broader tract, including Sherwood Forest, the soil of which is chiefly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> and gravelly; but though naturally sterile, it has in some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> been brought into a productive state by the extensive cultivation of turnips, and the maintenance of considerable flocks of sheep. The tract which adjoins is a clayey soil, extending to the banks of the River Trent. It is chiefly arable land, but varied with woods and meadows, and highly productive of wheat, oats, beans, and, in some parts, of hops. The lands on the banks of the Trent are very fertile, being mostly devoted to pasture, on which many oxen are fattened; and some of the dairies are extensive. The arable land of this district is celebrated both for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the oats which it produces. The beautiful vale of Belvoir, in the south-easternmost part of the county, enjoys some of the best soils, both for pasture and arable husbandry, of any part of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. The farms are in general small, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> held by tenants at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a>, the rents taken from whom are generally moderate; and a very <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> proportion of the land is free from the burden of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>. The spirit of agricultural improvement has not proceeded so far as in many other counties, though it has made considerable progress of late years. Neither the breeds of cows and sheep nor the modes of cultivation differ so much from those of the adjoining counties as to deserve any especial notice. There are no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> except those of coal, which are exclusively confined to a narrow district bordering on Derbyshire; the coal is of good quality, very abundant, and, by means of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RAILWAYS">railways</a> and internal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, diffused throughout the whole county. Excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is raised in many parts, some of which has the peculiarly valuable quality of hardening by exposure to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. Many parts of the county abound in veins of gypsum. In the parish of Gotham it is found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of the thickness of 3 feet. At Beaconhill, near Newark, there are large quarries of this substance. Although it has been much praised as a manure, the trials of it that have been made in its vicinity have not been attended with such beneficial results as to induce the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it for that purpose. It should only be used in moderate quantity, and on stiff soils. The forest of Sherwood, formerly celebrated as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of the exploits of Robin Hood, whose deeds amused our nursery days, is mostly an open heathy plain, bordered with recent plantations, and upon which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> has made very extensive encroachments. The boundaries of the forest are extensive, it being 25 miles in length, and from 7 to 9 in breadth; but a great portion of it has become the property of private individuals, and is inclosed in farms and parks; in the latter of which is to be found the deer with which this forest was once most abundantly stocked. The trees of most <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> date are those on the estates of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Mansvers. Nottinghamshire is, for its population, one of the greatest manufacturing counties. (For information on this subject the reader is referred to the concluding part of the article Nottingham.) The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> of cotton-yarn, from its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> connection with the trade of the district, has been introduced and very widely extended; and the establishments at Nottingham, at Pleasley Works, near Mansfield, and several other places, are upon an extensive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>. There are also some large manufactories for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a>-throwing and for spinning worsted yarn. Malting and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREWING">brewing</a> are carried on to a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; and the beer of Nottingham and of Newark rivals that of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-BURTON_UPON_TRENT">Burton-upon-Trent</a>. There are potteries at Sutton-in-Ashfield; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STARCH">starch</a> is made at Lenton; and sailcloth and candlewick at Retford. The foreign trade of this county is mostly conducted by the mercantile houses of London and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>; but some of the larger manufacturers export their own goods both to the continent of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and to the more distant parts of the world. The River Trent, the fourth in magnitude of the English streams, passes across the county, and is navigable for barges throughout the whole of it; but its deficiencies of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> and its shoals are such great <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-IMPEDIMENTS">impediments</a> that a canal by the side of it, 10 miles in length, is found of great use to the intercourse. The other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are not navigable, but are beneficial for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRRIGATION">irrigation</a>. They are the Erewash, the Soar, the Maun, the Meden, the Wollen, the Worksop, the Idle, the Leen, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> or Dare. These all discharge their waters into the Trent. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> are—the Nottingham, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANTHAM">Grantham</a>, the Idle, and the Chesterfield. The last of these is about 40 miles in length; the others about 10 each. By means of these and the Trent, the intercourse by internal navigation is extended to almost every district of the county. In addition to this means of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>, all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> towns, and most of the more populous villages, are now embraced in the railway system. The titles derived from this county are those of Marquis of Granby, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Mansfield, Viscount Newark, and Barons Pierrepont and Carrington. For <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> purposes, the county has been divided into two districts, the northern and the southern. Each of them returns two members. The election for the northern <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> is held at Mansfield, and the polling-places are, that town, East Retford, and Nottingham. The election for the southern division is held at Newark, and the other polling-places are Bingham and Southwell. The three boroughs, Nottingham, Newark, and Retford, return each two members, as before the passing of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-REFORM">Reform</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BILL">Bill</a>. The whole of the county is in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, to which it was transferred from that of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORK">York</a> at the recommendation of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> commissioners in 1836. It is on the midland circuit of the judges. The remains of Roman and Norman antiquities are numerous. Amongst the former are the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a> at Barton Hill, at Combes <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARM">Farm</a>, at Gringley, at Hexgrave, and at Wenney Hill, and a Roman villa near Mansfield. Among the latter are the Castle of Newark; the abbeys of Newstead, Rufford, and Welbeck; the priories of Mattersey and Worksop; and the churches of Bingham, Blythe, Southwell, and Balderton. Among the distinguished natives of this county have been Archbishop Cranmer, Dr Erasmus Darwin, Sir Martin Frobisher, Denzil Lord Holles, Ireton, the son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of Cromwell, Lady <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Wortley Montague, Paul Sandby, Archbishop Secker, Gilbert <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAKEFIELD">Wakefield</a>, Bishop Warburton, and Henry Kirke <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">White</a>. The seats of noblemen and gentlemen of the first class are as numerous as in any county of England. Among the most remarkable are the following, viz.:—Annesley <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>, John Musters, Esq.; Babworth Hall, H. B. Simpson, Esq.; Bramcote Hall, J. S. Sherwin, Esq.; Bunny <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARK">Park</a>, G. A. Forteath, Esq.; Clifton <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GROVE">Grove</a>, Sir Robert J. Clifton; Clumber Park, Duke of Newcastle; Colwick Hall (unoccupied); Elton <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANOR">Manor</a>, W. F. N. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol13.html#article-NORTON">Norton</a>, Esq.; Flintham Hall, T. B. T. Hildyard, Esq.; Grove Hall, G. H. <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VERNON">Vernon</a>, Esq.; Holme Pierrepont, Viscount Newark, M.P.; Kelham <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, J. H. M. Sutton, Esq.; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a> Hall, Lord <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BELPER">Belper</a>; Mapperley House, Ichabod Wright, Esq.; Newstead <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>, late Lord Byron (now <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Wildman); Norwood Park, Sir John Sutton, Bart.; Nuttall Temple, R. Holden, Esq.; Osberton, George S. Foljambe, Esq.; Osington Hall, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">Honourable</a> J. E. Denison, M.P.; Oxton Grange, H. P. Sherbrooke, Esq.; Ruddington Grange, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Paget, Esq., M.P.; Rempstone Hall, Lady Sitwell; Rufford Abbey, Earl of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCARBOROUGH">Scarborough</a>; Serlby Hall, Viscount <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GALWAY">Galway</a>, M.P.; Stanford Hall, Rev. S. V. Dashwood; Thoresby Park, Earl Manvers; Thrump-

NOUREDIN

Pages 348-349
or NOOR-ED-DEEN, the name of several Moslem rulers of Syria, of whom the most distinguished was Noureddin Mahmoud, Melik-El-Adel, who succeeded his father the famous Zenghi, Emir of Aleppo, in 1146. His reign was endangered at its commencement by the attempts of the Christians to regain the possessions which had lately been wrested from them. Josceline de Courtenay seized upon his former capital Edessa; but he was speedily dislodged, and the rebellious spirit of the citizens was suppressed by an extensive massacre. The second crusade, under the command of Louis VII. of France and the Emperor Conrad, arrived in 1148. But the ranks of the Christian invaders had been wasted in their march by the shafts and scimitars of the infidels; their strength was now still further weakened by the dissensions of the royal leaders; and after sitting down for some time before Damascus, they returned ignominiously to Europe. It was about this time that Noureddin conceived the grand project of rearing an effectual barrier against future crusades by annihilating the dominion of the Christians in Palestine, and uniting all Syria and the neighbouring districts under one government. For achieving such an enterprise his character peculiarly qualified him. His pious zeal had raised him high in the estimation of his fellow-Moslems; his conscientious frugality specially adapted him for the management of military expeditions; on account of his majestic bearing and simple soldier-like manners, he had become the darling of his army; and for his just rule and merciful care for the poor and the oppressed, he was regarded as the father of his people. Accordingly, he began the enterprise with great vigour and success. Raymond, Prince of Antioch, was defeated and slain in 1149; Josceline de Courtenay, Count of Edessa, was taken captive soon afterwards; and the whole of Northern Syria became in consequence the possession of Noureddin. He then turned his attention to the gaining of Damascus. The course of events rendered force in this case unnecessary. Anar, the able vizier of that kingdom, died; the ruler Moutjir-Ed-Deen was considered too imbecile to resist the threatened attack of Baldwin III., King of Jerusalem; and in 1154 the terrified inhabitants of Damascus willingly put themselves under the jurisdiction of the powerful and benign Emir of Aleppo. Noureddin had now extended his dominions around the borders of the Latin territories in Palestine, and had thus gained a favourable position for carrying out still further the great project of his reign. A severe illness, indeed, in 1159, and a defeat which the Christians inflicted upon him, gave a check to his success. But speedily recovering himself, he encountered the famous Reginald de Chatillon, prince of Antioch, defeated him, and took him prisoner. Taking advantage also of the distracted state into which the khalifate of Egypt had been plunged by the contention for the viziership between two emirs, Shawir and Ed-Dirgham, he resolved to extend his influence into that country. Sheerkooh, and his nephew Salah-Ed-Deen or Saladin, were accordingly despatched at the head of an army to raise the former of the rivals to the contested office. At first the enterprise was unsuccessful. Shawir, after he had been placed in the viziership, refused to fulfil his obligations to Sheerkooh, and summoned in aid of Amaury, the son and successor of Baldwin III. The troops of Aleppo were besieged in Pelusium, and were forced to capitulate to the Christians. At length, however, the tactics of Noureddin himself retrieved the declining fortunes of the Moslems. His inroad into the state of Antioch recalled Amaury to its defence; the Christian troops immediately on their arrival were routed near Tiresia with disastrous loss; and Sheerkooh being sent once more into Egypt, succeeded, in 1168, in removing the perfidious Shawir by death, and in establishing himself as lieutenant of Egypt in the name of his master. The schismatic khalifate of the Fatimites in that country was then abolished; the Egyptians were restored to the spiritual jurisdiction of the Abasside khaliph of Baghdad; and that chief of the Faithful conferred upon his meritorious servant Noureddin the title of Sultan, and the direct investiture of Egypt and Syria. Noureddin might now have turned his vastly increased resources against the Latin states in Palestine, and might thus have achieved the magnificent result to which all his past successes had been tending. But the last few years of his life were molested by the ambitious intrigues of the able Salah-Ed-Deen, who had succeeded his uncle Sheerkooh in the lieutenancy of Egypt. He was on the eve of setting out to chastise his rebellious subject, when an attack of quinsy brought his days to a close at Damascus in May 1173.

NOVA SCOTIA

Pages 350-353

a British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, situated between N. Lat. 43° 25' and 46° 0', and W. Lon. 61° 0' and 66° 30', and connected with the S.E. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the continent by an isthmus of only 8 miles in width. It is bounded on the N. by the Strait of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, which divides it from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Edward's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>; on the N.E. by the Gut of Canseau, which interposes between it and the island of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Breton; on the S. and S.E. by the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic Ocean</a>; on the W. by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> of Fundy; and on the N.W. by New <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> length, from Cape Canseau on the E. to Cape St <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s on the W., is about 280 miles; but its breadth varies from 50 to about 100 miles; and it contains a superficies of 15,607 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. From this, however, about one-fifth may be deducted for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, arms of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, leaving about 8,000,000 acres of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, the greater part of which is still uncleared, and covered with forests. The most remarkable characteristic of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> is Surface. The numerous indentations along the coasts. The shores are lined with rocks, and studded with thousands of small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to these, and in the harbours, almost without exception, there is a considerable depth of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>. All along the S.E. shore there is a succession of noble harbours; and vessels sail amongst and within the myriads of islands which line the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> during the most blustering <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, thus enjoying comparatively smooth water, whilst the main ocean heaves in violent agitation. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inlets are Sheet Harbour, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a> Harbour, Margaret's Bay, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAHON">Mahon</a> Bay, Shelburne Harbour, on the Atlantic; St Mary's Bay, 10 miles <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and 35 <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANNAPOLIS">Annapolis</a> Basin, 10 miles in length, and from 1 to 4 in breadth; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">Mines</a> Basin, 50 miles long, and 16 broad at the widest part, on the Bay of Fundy, which is terminated by Chignecto Bay, between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick; Picton Harbour, on Northumberland Strait; St George's Bay, on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a> of St Lawrence; and Chedabucto Bay, on the Gut of Cansau. Between Halifax and Cape Cansean there are said to be no less than twelve harbours capable of accommodating ships of the line, besides fourteen others accessible for merchantmen. The interior of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is very agreeably diversified with hill and dale, river and lake, forest and grassy plain. The surface, although undulating, is not mountainous; the highest land, Ardoise Hill <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>'s Seat, being only 810 feet above the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the sea, nearly the same height as Arthur's Seat at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> lands generally run <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the coasts, branching off in all directions, and in some instances terminating in bold cliffs on the coast, the most remarkable of which is Aspotagoo, between Mahon and Margaret's Bay, which is about 500 feet in height. A tract of rugged and hilly country stretches along the shore of the Atlantic, varying in breadth from 20 to 60 miles, and having an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> height of about 500 feet. The North <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, which are washed by the Mines Basin, extend along the coast of the Bay of Fundy, and terminate in Cape Blomidon; and parallel to these run the South Mountains in the interior of the peninsula. The Cobequid Hills extend from the northern shores of Mines Basin towards Northumberland Strait, having a breadth of 10 miles, and a height of about 800 feet. There are several remarkable caverns and grottoes in Nova Scotia, one of which, at St <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s Point, on the coast of the Bay of Fundy, displays in the interior a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of which is fretted with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STALACTITES">stalactites</a>. The interior of Nova Scotia is intersected and watered by numerous rivers, lakes, and streams, which beautify and enrich the country. The two largest rivers are the Annapolis and the Shubenacadie. The former takes its rise in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">County</a>, and, running parallel with the Bay of Fundy, after a long and serpentine course, in which it receives the Moose and Bear Rivers, discharges itself into Annapolis Bay. It is navigable to a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and its banks present a rich and pleasing landscape. The Shubenacadie, issuing from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Lake in the county of Halifax, divides that county from Hants, and, after a rapid and circuitous course, the length of which has not yet been accurately ascertained, discharges itself into the Bay of Mines. It receives the waters of ten other rivers, is navigable for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessels a long way into the interior, and contains on its banks inexhaustible quantities of gypsum and lime, together with extensive groves of fine <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. At Pictou, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THREE_RIVERS">three rivers</a>, navigable for large vessels, empty themselves into the harbour; the East, West, and Middle Rivers. Besides these, there are the Avon, navigable for a considerable distance; the La Have, which issues from a chain of inland lakes, and has a course of about 60 miles; the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>, which winds from Lake Rosignol through the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN_S_COUNTY"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s county, and discharges itself into <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a> Harbour; the Medway, the Shelburne, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, the Tusket, the St Mary, and others, all of which owe their origin to lakes in the interior. A canal, called the Shubenacadie Canal, together with a chain of lakes, forms a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> by water across the peninsula from Halifax Harbour to Cobequid Bay, at the head of the Mines Basin. The most extensive still sheet of water is the Rosignol, situated partly in each of the three counties of Queen, Shelburne, and Annapolis. It is said to be 30 miles in length, but is little known. Lake George is also of considerable size; and there are innumerable others which it is unnecessary to mention. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Nova Scotia was for many years after its discovery considered as an insuperable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> to agricultural industry, and an idea long prevailed in England that it was peculiarly the region of snow and fog. The temperature is indeed colder in winter in this peninsula than it is in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; but when the weather is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a> it is usually dry; and altogether the winter is milder, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> less intensely hot, than at Quebec. The summer <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is moderate and regular; the autumn is a delightful season; and there is seldom any severe winter weather until the end of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FROST">Frost</a> continues generally from Christmas to April, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> is of very short <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. The temperature varies during the year from 6° or 8° Fahr. below zero, to 80° above it, the average of the coldest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> at Halifax being about 20°, and that of the hottest about 70°. Like other parts of North America, however, Nova Scotia is subject to sudden changes of temperature, sometimes as much as 50° in twenty-four hours. The mildness of the climate seems to be owing in some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to the influence of the gulf-stream, which prevents the harbours on the Atlantic from being frozen up in winter like those on the northern coast. There is a great variety of rocks in Nova Scotia; but <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, trap, and clay-slate predominate. The most abundant variety is the gray granite, which, together with gneiss and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MICA">mica</a>-slate, prevails along the shore, and is well adapted for mill-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Trap rocks, sometimes embedded in clay-slate, protrude in various places in immense parallel ridges above the surface, and frequently in piles of loose masses heaped confusedly together, traversed frequently by veins of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-QUARTZ">quartz</a>. Clay-slate of a very fine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and used as a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, prevails in the eastern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of the colony; and graywacke and graywacke-slate extend along both shores of Chedabucto Bay, in which are found beds of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> and numerous specimens of specular <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> ore. In connection with carboniferous limestone are found, both in Cape Breton and Nova Scotia, those immense coal-fields which are supposed to rival in extent the mines of the mother country. The coal is of a bituminous character, and entirely different from that which is found in the United States, east of the Appalachian Mountains. It is of various kinds, some of which are well fitted for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the smith, others for that of steamboats, and others for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAS">gas</a>-making. In the coal formations of this country there is also found an immense <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of gypsum, which is largely exported to the United States. Varieties of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, iron, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> ores are also abundant; and different other minerals of less importance are found. Fine specimens of agates, amethysts, chalcedonies, jaspers, and other stones, are obtained in Nova Scotia. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">Salt</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, some of them strongly impregnated with saline <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, are met with near Pictou, at River <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, and some other parts. The wild animals are the moose, cariboo, bear, lynx, fox, marten, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OTTER">otter</a>, mink, beaver, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RAT">rat</a>, porcupine, raccoon, weasel, squirrel, hare, and the like, all of which, excepting the two last, have rapidly decreased in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. Nearly all the birds <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to North America frequent Nova Scotia; and there are but very few kinds of fish which are found in the American seas that do not frequent the shores of this colony in vast swarms. The lakes and rivers abound in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a> and salmon. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is of many different qualities, and various degrees of fertility. The alluvial or intervale lands, of which there are extensive tracts, are rich, and produce plentiful returns of wheat, barley, oats, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn, potatoes, turnips, with all the vegetables and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> common in England. Some of the uplands, lying between the hilly country and the rivers, are <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; whilst the high lands are rich and very productive. The lands on the Atlantic coast are generally so rocky as to admit of cultivation only at much expense and labour; but after the stones are removed, the soil is by no means barren. The forests of Nova Scotia still constitute a prominent feature of the country. The trees are the same as those common to America, and the timber is generally large and lofty. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> is carried on to a considerable extent in Nova Scotia. The cultivated ground consists partly of the rich alluvial marshes on the shore of the Bay of Fundy, and partly of the uplands in the interior of the country. The former kind of ground, which has been recovered from the sea by means of dykes, was estimated in 1850 to amount to 40,012 acres; and the latter to 799,310 acres. The produce in 1852 was 297,157 bushels of wheat, 196,097 of barley, 61,488 of rye, 1,384,437 of oats, 170,301 of buckwheat, 37,475 of maize, 21,638 of pease and beans, 3686 of grass seeds, 1,986,789 of potatoes, 467,127 of turnips, 32,325 of other roots, 257,837 tons of hay, 3,613,890 lb. of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, and 625,069 lb. of cheese. The amount of live stock in the same year was 28,789 horses, 156,857 neat cattle, 86,586 milch cows, 282,180 sheep, and 51,533 swine. Sable Island, although distant about 85 miles from Nova Scotia, is considered as belonging to that province. It lies directly in the track of vessels bound to or from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and has been the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of numerous and melancholy shipwrecks. It is 25 miles in length, by about 1¼ in breadth, the eastern end being in Lat. 43° 59' N., and Long. 59° 45' W. It is a barren <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> throughout, the soil consisting chiefly of sand, and the only vegetable productions being a coarse grass and some wild pease. A sum, which amounted in 1854 to L.1977, is annually devoted to keeping on the island a superintendent from Nova Scotia, with a party of men provided with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and other necessaries, for the purpose of affording assistance to any shipwrecked mariners, of whatsoever <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, who may be driven on its inhospitable shores. There is a small stock of cattle on the island, and a large number of wild horses, but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> supplies of food are obtained from Nova Scotia. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are few in number, consisting principally of coarse cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a>, carpets, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, spirits, and agricultural implements. The province contained in 1850, 1,153 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, employing 1,786 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; 386 grist-mills, employing 437 hands; 10 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>-mills; 237 tanneries; 9 foundries; 81 carding and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a> establishments; 17 breweries and distilleries; and 131 other manufactories of various sorts. In the same year there were raised in Nova Scotia 114,992 chaldrons of coal; there were quarried 79,795 tons of gypsum, valued at L.10,498; 28,603 casks of lime, valued at L.4,433, were burned; 2,845,400 bricks, valued at L.3211, were made; and 110,441 lb. of maple <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> were produced. In the same year the value of leather manufactured was L.52,625; of boots and shoes, L.73,654; of iron smelted, L.4635; of castings, L.3486; of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, L.28,277; and of candles, L.21,210. Ship-building is also carried on in Nova Scotia. The number of vessels constructed in 1854 was 244, and their tonnage 52,814. Besides farming, the chief occupation of the inhabitants is <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>; and some combine both pursuits. There were in 1851 employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a> of Nova Scotia and Cape Breton 812 vessels, with a tonnage of 43,333, and manned by 3681 men; 5161 boats, with 6713 men; and the number of nets and seines was 30,154. The quantity of fish cured was 196,484 quintals; and there were also obtained 1669 barrels of salmon; 3386 of shad; 100,047 of mackerel; 53,200 of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>; 5343 of alewives; and 15,409 boxes of smoked herrings, valued at L.217,270; as well as 189,250 gallons of fish <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, valued at L.17,754. The total value of the fisheries is estimated to exceed L.200,000. The exports of the province consist principally of fish, sugar, molasses, rum, cotton and woollen goods, timber, &c. The total value of the exports in 1854 was L.1,247,668. The principal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> imported are flour, sugar, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, manufactured goods, &c.; the total value of the imports in 1854 was L.1,791,082. The number and tonnage of the vessels that entered and cleared in 1851 were as follows: | Countries | Entered | Cleared | |--------------------|---------|---------| | United <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">Kingdom</a> | 107 | 74 | | British Colonies | 1447 | 1045 | | United States | 1831 | 159 | | Other Countries | 267 | 208 | | Total | 3402 | 3247 | The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a> in Nova Scotia is in the hands of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a>-governor, and a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of six members. The legislature consists of a council of nineteen, appointed by the governor, subject to the approval of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">Assembly</a>, of fifty-one members, elected by the people. The system of responsible <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> has been established in Nova Scotia since 1848. The lieutenant-governor has a salary of L.3000 a-year. The judicial establishment consists of a supreme <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, composed of a chief-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and four assistant judges; which sits at Halifax three times a-year, and makes two annual circuits of the province; a court of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, composed of the lieutenant-governor and executive council; a court of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>; courts of general sessions of the peace; courts of vice-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>; a court of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> and divorce; and courts of probate. The established <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is Episcopalian; Nova Scotia was created a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> in 1787, and has a bishop, an archdeacon, and fifty other clergymen; the two first being supported by an endowment from the home government, and the others by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> for the Propagation of the Gospel. The amount of public expenditure for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> purposes in 1854 was L.3687. There is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SYNOD">Synod</a> of Nova Scotia in connection with the Established <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> of Scotland, and various churches in connection with the Free Church of Scotland and the United Presbyterian Church. The Roman Catholic Church has two dioceses, Nova Scotia and Cape Breton, within the province. The whole number of churches in 1851 was 567; and the adherents of the various denominations were as follows: - Church of England: 33,482 - Church of Scotland: 18,857 - Free Church of Scotland: 25,280 - United <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>: 28,767 - <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>: 69,634 Nova Scotia contains several colleges, besides inferior educational establishments. King's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a> resembles the English <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and Dalhousie College at Halifax those of Scotland. There are also a Free Church college, a Baptist college, and a Roman Catholic college. None of the attempts which have been made to unite some of these colleges into a university has proved successful. Each of the counties in the province has a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school; and the total number of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> in Nova Scotia in 1851 was 1086, attended by 31,354 scholars. The amount of public <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONEY">money</a> expended on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in 1854 was L.13,401. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> forces of the province consist of twenty-six <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">Army</a>-regiments of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, 26,248 strong, but which might soon be raised to nearly <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> that number. Besides this, Nova Scotia is protected by two or three regiments of the line, which are always stationed in the garrison <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and by the visits during the summer of the squadron of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NAVY">Navy</a>. The principal fortifications in the province... The inhabitants of Nova Scotia consist of English, Scotch, Irish, Americans, Germans, Swiss, Acadian French, Indians, and freed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">Negroes</a>. They mingle and live together in much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>, and generally the social state of the province is rapidly improving. Its prosperity has greatly increased; and, instead of importing, it now exports provisions. Its fisheries, to which proper <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is at length paid, its rich and prolific soil, and its mines of coal and iron, are sources of wealth which were too long neglected by Great Britain. The province is divided into eighteen counties, including Cape Breton, as follows: | Counties | Pop. (1831) | Capitals | |----------------|-------------|----------| | Halifax | 39,112 | Halifax | | <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LUNENBURG">Lunenburg</a> | 16,395 | Lunenburg| | Queen's | 7,256 | Liverpool| | Shelburne | 10,622 | Shelburne| | <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a> | 13,142 | Yarmouth | | Digby | 12,252 | Digby | | Annapolis | 14,286 | Annapolis| | Kentville | 14,138 | Kentville| | Windsor | 14,330 | Windsor | | <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMHERST">Amherst</a> | 14,339 | Amherst | | <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRURO">Truro</a> | 15,469 | Truro | | Antigonish | 25,593 | Antigonish| | Guysborough | 13,457 | Guysborough| | Port Hood | 10,831 | Port Hood| | Arichat | 16,917 | Arichat | | <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYDNEY">Sydney</a> | 10,381 | Sydney | | Bedeque | 27,580 | Bedeque | Total: 276,117 Our limits <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> only admit of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Nova Scotia. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> authorities state that it was discovered by the Cabots in 1497; but it was not until 1604 that the French attempted to form settlements. They were, however, expelled from it in 1614 by the English colonists of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, who claimed the country in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of the discovery of Sebastian Cabot. In 1621 Sir William Alexander obtained a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of the whole peninsula, and it was named in the patent Nova Scotia, instead of Acadia, as the country was called by the French. In the meantime the latter obtained a footing in it a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and it was not until 1654, when a strong force was despatched by Cromwell, that the French settlers were brought under subjection. In 1667 Nova Scotia was ceded to France by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREDA">Breda</a>; but, after suffering during the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> which broke out in 1701, as well as previously, it was finally ceded to England by treaty in the year 1711. From this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> till 1749 it was neglected by Great Britain; but the designs of the French called the attention of government to the province. Encouragements were held out to settlers; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a> gave a large grant; and about 4000 adventurers, with their families, embarked for the colony. Halifax was immediately founded; but the French settlers, under the name of neutrals, were still very numerous; and, with the aid of the Indians, they inflicted repeated injuries upon the British, until they were forcibly expelled by the latter. In 1758 a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was granted to Nova Scotia; and the capture of Louisburg, in the island of Cape Breton, during the same year, gave additional security to the colony, which now began to improve. By the treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 10th of February 1762, France resigned all further claims on any of her former possessions in North America, and nothing of any material importance has since occurred. New Brunswick and Cape Breton were separated from Nova Scotia, and formed into two distinct governments, in 1784, but the latter was re-annexed to Nova Scotia in 1819.

NOVA ZEMBLA

Pages 353-354
or Novaya Zemlya, a name which signifies in Russian “New Land,” is applied to an island, or rather chain of islands, in the Arctic Ocean. It extends from N.N.E. to S.S.W., curving slightly towards the W., and lies between N. Lat. 70° 30' and 76° 30', E. Long. 51° 30' and 77°. It is washed on the W. by the Spitzbergen Sea, and on the E. by the Kara Sea; which, along with Burrough's Strait, separates Nova Zembla from the continent and from the island of Vaigats. Its whole length is about 500 miles, with an average breadth of about 50. The most southerly island of the chain is separated from the rest by a strait called Matochkin Shar, or Matthew's Strait; and farther to the N. there is another strait called Cross Bay, which divides itself into several arms, and forms other small islands. The southern island alone is properly called Nova Zembla; the middle one, which is much smaller, is known by the name of Matthew's Land; while to the N. lie Lütke's Land and Barent's Land, believed to form one continuous island. The eastern shores of all the islands are low; but on the W. the land is mountainous, rising in general 2000 feet above the sea, and the highest summit, near Matthew's Strait, is 3475 feet in height. The formation of the mountain is for the most part black clay-slate; and in the southern islands grey limestone, like that of the northern part of the Ural chain. The climate of these islands is indicated by the following table: | Place | N. Lat. | E. Long. | Mean Annual Temp. | Mean Summer Temp. | Mean Winter Temp. | |---------------------|---------|----------|-------------------|------------------|------------------| | South extremity | 79° 37' | 47° | 16° 29' | 35° 59' | 3° 21' | | Matthew's Strait | 73° | 20° | 16° 93' | 38° 49' | 2° 29' | | Cross Bay | 74° | 0° | 20° 74' | 36° 60' | 9° 78' | The vegetation is very scanty, consisting only of mosses and lichens; in many parts the ground is quite barren; and notwithstanding the long continuance of the sun above the horizon, the soil is never thawed more than a foot or two deep. Animal life is as scarce here as vegetation. Nova Zembla is often visited by fishermen from Archangel in pursuit of the walrus. It was visited at an early period by the Russians, but was first brought into notice by Steven Burrough, who made a voyage thither in 1556. The west and part of the east coast were visited in 1596 by the Dutch navigator Barents; and several Russian expeditions have been sent out from Russia within the present century to explore the islands. NOVEL. See ROMANCE, part ii.

NOVALIS

Pages 349-350

the literary pseudonym usually applied to Friedrich Ludwig von Hardenberg, a distinguished <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and poet of Germany, who was born at a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of his family in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Mansfeld, in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, on the 2d of May 1772. His father, a frank, rugged, honest German, had spent his early years as a soldier, but was at this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-works. The mother of Novalis was "a pattern of noble piety and Christian mildness," and her son seems to have loved her with the most enthusiastic affection.
