From both his parents, who were attached to the Herrnhut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, Novalis inherited that decidedly <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> temper which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be the ruling principle of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In childhood he was very delicate, and was brought up in the most retired manner. He showed no <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in the boisterous sports of youth, and even shunned the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of his fellows. He remained in this dull, dreamy condition until his ninth year, when a dangerous illness shook his faculties from their slumber, and called forth the energies of a genius of uncommon power and originality. His elementary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> was now prosecuted with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success; and he displayed an extraordinary fondness for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. The Tradtionary Tale (Märchen), which he afterwards continued to admire, had at this early stage a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> for him; and one of his earliest literary endeavours was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of this sort, written for the amusement of his brothers and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>. After a few months at a gymnasium, he repaired to Jena in 1790, where he prosecuted his studies for three years. He then removed with his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Erasmus to the university of Leipzig, and after spending a season there, went to Wittemberg to complete his education. It seems to have been Jena, however, which exerted the most marked influence over his development. Here he first met Friedrich Schlegel, and it was here he first listened to the lofty eloquence of Fichte. The Wissenschaftstlehre, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Doctrine of Science, of that distinguished thinker, was studied by Novalis with singular avidity. The charm of its refined idealism attracted the sympathies of an intellect of surprising subtlety; the stern <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of its morality called forth the enthusiasm of the youthful romanticist; and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> eloquence and calm <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of the teacher carried conviction to the heart of the student. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of Fichte formed accordingly the groundwork of all the subsequent speculations of Novalis. The Kantian distinction, and even occasional antagonism, of the Understanding and the Reason, is carried by him into all departments of mental development—into poetry, virtue, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. He learned to despise with the transcendentalists the dull, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, pedestrianism of the Understanding, and sought to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the citadel of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> by following the clear, steady <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the higher Reason. The whole of his writings have a constant reference to this specula- After displaying a strong predilection for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> life, his friends succeeded in prevailing on him to follow his father's occupation; and he accordingly removed to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARNSTADT">Arnstadt</a> in Thuringia in 1794, to train himself for business. Having remained a year there, he was appointed auditor of the department of which his father was director, and took up his residence at Weissenfels. In the year 1797 events occurred which, according to his biographer Tieck, gave a shock to his whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and imparted a gloomy <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> to his thoughts, from which he was not destined to recover. During his residence at Arnstadt he had become enamoured of a fair, delicate German girl, possessed of uncommon attractions, but with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> exceedingly fragile. He had hardly known her a year when the chill <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> winds came and withered the fair flower; and ere he had time to dry his tears, he had to follow the remains of his brother Erasmus to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>. It was during this year that the greater <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those remarkable pieces of Novalis, called *Hymns to the Night*, were composed. Not a few of his *Fragments* also belong to the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. In 1798 he removed to Freyberg to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">mineralogy</a> under the famous Werner. In the mathematical and physical sciences he took an eager interest; and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may judge from the fragmentary papers which he has left, he seemed to have prosecuted the study on a great and original principle. He put together about this time his unfinished "physical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>" of *Lehringe zu Saiz*, or the Pupils at Sais, so full of strange poetized philosophy and shadowy allegorical allusion. While here he formed another betrothment, destined like the first to be cut short by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. On his return to Jena he made the acquaintance of August Wilhelm Schlegel and Tieck, then engaged in the famous literary <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> in behalf of what is generally known as Romanticism. Tieck "re-awakened poetry in him," he says; and it was in conjunction with these men, whose cause he ardently espoused, that Novalis first presented his thoughts to the world. He contributed his *Blüthensaub*, or Pollen of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">Flowers</a>, together with numerous poetical pieces, to the *Musen-Almanach* of F. Schlegel; and composed about the same time his *Geistliche Lieder*, or Spiritual Songs, so remarkable for simple sublimity and still, devout pathos. In addition to his passionate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of nature, these were perhaps his highest poetic gifts. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of 1800 we find him living at a solitary spot at the foot of the Kyffhäuser Mountain in Thuringia, busily engaged on his art romance of *Heinrich von Ofterdingen*, designed, as he said, to be an "<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a> of Poetry." It was never completed, however, and was not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> published in its unfinished state. In his prose style he generally aims at simplicity and directness—qualities not always to be found in his poetry. Indeed, it may be questioned whether, with all the wealth of a truly regal genius, he was possessed of the highest faculties of the poet. If in the rich strength of his theosophic mysticism he resembles an oriental, the likeness is increased when we regard the soft passiveness of his mind and character. Carlyle, who calls him the "German Pascal," says, "The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> excellence we have remarked in Novalis is his, to us, truly wonderful subtlety of intellect; his power of intense abstraction, of pursuing the deepest and most evanescent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> through their thousand complexities, as it were with lynx vision, and to the very limits of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> thought." (*Miscellanies*, vol. ii., p. 95.) In August 1800, while Novalis was preparing for a journey to Freyberg to bring home his betrothed, he was seized with a spitting of blood, which ended in a rapid decline. Hope, gladness, and rich expanding <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> had <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> begun to make life desirable to him, when death came with the spring of 1801, and ended his strange <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a>, at the premature <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of twenty-eight. A Life of Novalis, by his friend Tieck, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found prefixed to

NOVARA

Pages 350-350

a town in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">Kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the same name, stands on a rising ground between the Agogna and the Terdoppio, 63 miles E.N.E. of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>. It is well built, containing several good and well-paved streets; and was formerly surrounded by walls, but these have now nearly all disappeared. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and handsome <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> tower surmounted by a cupola, and contains in the interior several fine paintings and sculptures. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St. Gaudenzio is likewise a fine structure, and contains one of the best paintings of Gaudenzio Ferrari. Besides these and other churches, Novara contains public offices, a town-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>-house, an episcopal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> and seminary, several upper <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>, and market-house. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> are not very extensive, and consist chiefly of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, cotton cloth, candles, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POTTERY">pottery</a>, and biscuits. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> trade is in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and rural produce, for the latter of which Novara is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> emporium in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>. Near the town a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> was fought in 1849, in which the Sardinians were totally defeated by the Austrians under Radetzky. The result of this engagement was the resignation of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Sardinia by the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a>, Carlo Alberto, and the renunciation of the Sardinia claims on <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>. Pop. about 16,000. The division of Novara is bounded on the N. by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, E. by Lake Maggiore and the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TICINO">Ticino</a>, S. by the Po, and W. by the divisions of Turin and Ivrea. Towards the N.W. it is occupied by the branches of the Alps; but the greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> consists of a fertile plain, watered by the Foza, Sesia, Terdoppio, Agogna, Ticino, and other smaller streams. Corn, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, &c., are grown here; and on the higher regions the vine is largely cultivated. The division of Novara is subdivided as follows: | Province | <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">Area</a> in sq. miles | Pop. (1830) | |----------|------------------|------------| | Novara | 533 | 178,069 | | Lemellina| 480 | 139,419 | | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALLANZA">Pallanza</a> | 312 | 64,020 | | Omegna | 560 | 35,321 | | Valenza | 290 | 35,879 | | **Total**| **2135** | **453,958**|

NOVATIANUS

Pages 353-353

the founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Novatians, was, according to Philostorgius, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, and was born about the beginning of the third century. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> intolerance of his opponents has falsified his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and has represented him as little else than a hypocritical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>-server. But the account which is most consistent with the growth of his peculiar opinions is the following:— His conversion took <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> after an intense mental struggle, and he was baptized when he was lying on a sick-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BED">bed</a>, in hourly <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. On his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, his religious sentiments retained a tinge of that gloom under which they had sprung into life. Admitted into the priesthood, he devoted himself to the severe theological studies and the ascetic penances of the cloister. It is not surprising, then, that his spirit was shocked at the easy terms on which those who had relapsed into idolatry during the Decian persecutions were re-admitted into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. He began to maintain boldly that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> had no warrant from Scripture to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> the sins of those who, after their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, had sacrificed to idols; that her sole duty in this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> was to exhort them to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>, and to commend them to the mercy of God. The learning, eloquence, and virtuous life of the new reformer soon drew a party around him. Among others, Novatus, a Carthaginian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, joined the dissentients, and by his hot-headed zeal speedily hurried the controversy into an open schism. Advantage was taken of the martyrdom of Fabianus, Bishop of Rome, in 250, to disown the authority of Cornelius, the successor to the vacant see, and to set up Novatianus as his rival. The result was, that at a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> convened at Rome in 251, the Novatians and their leader were excommunicated. Thus compelled to organize a new sect, the heresiarch set himself to develop his peculiar opinions. The following became the distinguishing tenets of his creed:—(1.) That not only sacrificing to idols, but all mortal sins, such as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a> and temporizing in any way with idolaters, ought to debar backsliders from re-admission into the church. (2.) That <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> this regulation were not maintained, the church would become defiled, and would no longer be (as it ought to be) a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a> who had never fallen since their baptism into any other than venial offences. This testimony Novatianus is said to have sealed with his blood. After his death, his followers, in spite of much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, rapidly increased and spread themselves over Christendom. They <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to vindicate their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to be considered the true church, by calling themselves καθολικοί (Puritans), and by re-baptizing all proselytes from other Christian sects. However, they did not maintain their existence as a separate sect for much longer than two centuries. Of the several works in which Novatianus displayed his methodical reasoning, his pure and elegant diction, and his animated style, three authenticated writings alone remain. These are a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> written in the name of the Roman clergy to Cyprian in 250, and two treatises entitled respectively De Trinitate, and De Cibis Judaicis. They have been published collectively by Welchman, 8vo, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, 1724, and by Jackson, 8vo, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1723. The two treatises are also generally found in the editions of Tertullian.

NOVELDA

Pages 354-354

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Alicante, and 15 miles W. of the town of that name. The streets are pretty regular, and the houses, which are mostly of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, are generally well built. Some trade in fruit and agricultural produce is carried on; and after <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, distilleries and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> principally afford employment to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, which amounts to about 9000.

NOVELLARA

Pages 354-354

a town of Northern <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, and 16 miles N.W. of the town of that name. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a principality annexed to Modena in 1737; and carries on some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. Pop. 4100.

NOVEMBER

Pages 354-354

the eleventh <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> year, was the ninth in the old Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>. On this account the name November <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Novembris (from novem, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a>) was assigned to it in the Alban calendar. It consisted originally of thirty days, but Julius Caesar added one to it. Augustus, however, again reduced it to its original <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, which it has ever since retained. (See CALENDAR.)

NOVGOROD

Pages 354-355
or Novogorod, a government of Russia, lying between N. Lat. 57° 18' and 61° 8', E. Long. 30° 10' and 39° 40.; and bounded on the N. by Olonetz, E. by Vologda and Yaroslavl, S. by Tver, and S.W., W., and N.W. by Pskov and St Petersburg; area, 46,833 square miles. The country is diversified with hills, valleys, plains, marshes, rivers, and lakes; the northern part is in general low and flat; but in the south the Valdai hills stretch for about 100 miles from S.W. to N.E., though these do not exceed 300 feet in height. The principal rivers are the Msta, which enters the government from Tver, flows north-west, and falls into Lake Ilmen; the Lovat, Pola, and Schelen, which fall into the same lake; the Volchov, which flows from that lake into the Ladoga Canal; the Schekona and Vologda, tributaries of the Volga; and the Sias and Buscha, which fall into Lake Ladoga. There are altogether in the government forty-two rivers, and fifty-five small, besides three large lakes. Of these last, the most extensive is the Bielo Ozero, or White Lake, in the north-east, which is 26 miles in length, about as much in breadth, and 432 square miles in extent. Lake Ilmen, near the western extremity, has a length of 26 miles, Novgorod, a breadth of 16, and an area of 346 square miles; and Lake Vosche has a length of 14 miles, and an area of 177 square miles. There is a canal, 5 miles in length, connecting the rivers Msta and Volchov, by which navigation is carried on without passing through Lake Ilmen, as that extensive sheet of water is liable to dangerous storms. The soil in the southern parts is good and productive; but in the north it is very swampy, consisting for the most part of peat bogs. The climate is cold, and the winter long, lasting from November to May; while in the northern parts the cold is extreme, and the winter about a month longer than in the south. A large part of the land is covered with dense forests of pine, fir, birch, alder, elm, and other trees, which supply abundance of timber for export, and give shelter to great numbers of deer, elks, bears, wolves, lynxes, and other wild animals. The people are chiefly engaged in agriculture; and the principal crops are rye, barley, oats, buckwheat, potatoes, peas, flax, and hemp. Although there is much fine pasture ground, the inclemency and length of the winters prevent the rearing of more cattle than is necessary for farming; horses, oxen, and sheep of the common Russian breeds, and a few goats and pigs, are kept. Next to agriculture, fishing is the most general occupation of the people; it is carried on with great success on the lakes and rivers. Coal, iron, freestone, slate, lime, marl, &c., are among the mineral produce of Novgorod; and there are also good salt springs. The manufactures are not very extensive; and consist of coarse linen, soap, candles, potash, &c. Distilling, iron-smelting, and bell-making are also carried on. The exports of the province consist entirely of home produce, especially corn, hemp, flax, iron, timber, salt, hides, and furs. The principal place of trade is Novgorod, the capital. The government is divided into ten circles. Pop. (1846) 907,900. Novgorod, the capital of the above government, stands on the Volchov, where it issues from Lake Ilmen, 120 miles S.S.E. of St Petersburg. It is one of the most ancient towns in Russia, having been founded in the fifth century of the Christian era by the Slavonians, who had long previously invaded Europe, and followed a wandering mode of life. Their government was at first democratic, but dissensions having broken out and greatly weakened their power, Ruric was invited in the ninth century to assume the government, and he established at Novgorod the original foundation of the Russian monarchy, the seat of which was soon afterwards removed to Kiev. Novgorod afterwards acquired many privileges from the Russian archdukes; and in the twelfth century became an independent republic under a hereditary magistrate of limited power. In the thirteenth century a factory of the Hanseatic League was established here; and for a long time Novgorod was the most important commercial city in the north-east of Europe. Its fairs were resorted to by the Hanse merchants, and by people from all the neighbouring countries; and in the fifteenth century it is said, though not probably with truth, to have contained 400,000 inhabitants. Indeed, so great was its power and prosperity at this time as to give rise to the saying, "Quis contra Deum et magnam Novgorodiam?" But this did not last long; for in 1477 its independence was completely destroyed by Ivan Vassilievich I.; and in 1570 Ivan IV. took occasion, from a reasonable correspondence of some of the citizens with Poland, to massacre more than 25,000 of the inhabitants. The trade of the place was still considerable, until the foundation of St Petersburg, which monopolized the Baltic trade, and completely destroyed the importance of Novgorod. It now presents most unmistakeable marks of fallen greatness in its ruinous buildings, dilapidated walls, and grassgrown streets. The Kremlin, or fortress, stands on the north side of the river, and is connected by a fine stone Novgorod-Sieversk, a town of Russia, capital of a district in the government of Tschernigov, stands on the right bank of the Desna, 109 miles E.N.E. of Tschernigov. It is surrounded by walls, and has a castle, but neither is in a good state of repair. An active trade in corn, hemp, and lime is carried on; and several large fairs are held annually. Pop. (1849) 10,544.

NOVI

Pages 355-355

a town of Northern <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a cognominal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, is situated in the plain of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARENGO">Marengo</a>, at the foot of the Apennines, 25 miles N.N.W. of Genoa. It is surrounded by an old dilapidated wall; and of its old castle few remains now exist. The streets are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> and narrow; but in the centre of the town is a handsome <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> adorned with a beautiful marble fountain. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> public <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a fine old edifice with two towers; and some of the old houses are noted for their picturesque appearance. It is the seat of civil and commercial tribunals; and has a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, two monasteries, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, and foundling <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. Novi has an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> trade; and carries on various <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, for which it is one of the most celebrated places in Italy. In the neighbourhood a severe <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a> took <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in 1799 between the French and Austro-Russians, in which the former were defeated. Pop. 10,300. The province has an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 288 square miles, and contained, in 1848, 65,013 inhabitants.

NOVI-BAZAR

Pages 355-355

a town of European <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a cognominal sanjak in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Bosnia, is situated on the Rashka, 130 miles S.E. of Bosna-Serbia. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of some trade; and has several warm <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. Pop. about 8000.

NOVICE

Pages 355-355

a person not yet skilled <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> experienced in an art or profession. In the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, novicii or noviti were the young raw <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, distinguished by this appellation from the veterans. In the ancient orders of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> there were novices or clerks in arms, who went through a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a> ere they were admitted knights. Novice is more particularly used in monasteries for a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> person in his or her noviciate or year of probation, and who has not taken the vows. In nunneries the novices wear a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a> veil, the rest a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> one. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of giving novices the religious dress was not known before the twelfth century. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a> fixed the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of profession at sixteen years.

NOVO-REDONDO

Pages 355-355

a seaport-town and port of S.W. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, belonging to the Portuguese. The town occupies the summit of a rock at the mouth of the River Redondo, and is inhabited almost solely by free <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">Negroes</a>. Novo-Tscherkask, a town of European Russia, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> Cossacks, on the River Don, about 40 miles from its mouth. It was founded in 1806 in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the unhealthiness of old Tscherkask, the then capital. It is the seat of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> offices; and is well laid out with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and regular streets, the houses being generally of one storey. It has a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> and numerous other churches, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. Pop. (1850) 17,875.

NOWAGURH

Pages 355-355

a raj of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, subject to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> for the S.W. frontier. Its centre is in Lat. 20.20. N., <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 82.25. E.; and it has an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 1512 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. Pop. estimated at 68,000. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is said to be among the worst governed of those within the circle to which it belongs.

NOWANUGGUR

Pages 355-355

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Katwyar, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Guzerat, 310 miles N.W. of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a>. It stands on a creek indenting the S. shore of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTCH">Cutch</a>; and carries on a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade, being the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the district of Hallar, which is estimated to contain a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of 207,680. The town itself is nearly 4 miles in circuit, and is celebrated for its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of fine cloth, as well as for the dyes given to that article. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">Copper</a> ore has been discovered in a range of hills in the vicinity.

NOX

Pages 355-355

one of the most <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> deities among the heathens, and the personification of Night. She was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHAOS">Chaos</a>, and from her union with her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EREBUS">Erebus</a>, she gave birth to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">Day</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>. She was also the mother of the Parcae, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HESPERIDES">Hesperides</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DREAMS">Dreams</a>; of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCORD">Discord</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">Death</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOMUS">Momus</a>, Fraud, &c. Nox is called by some of the poets the mother of all things, of gods as well as of men; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> makes her the subduer of gods and men, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-ZEUS">Zeus</a> himself being awed by her. (II. xiv.) She was worshipped with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> solemnity by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and had a famous statue, executed by Rhecius, in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> at Ephesus. It was usual to offer her a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> sheep, as she was the mother of the Furies; and a cock was also presented to her, as that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> proclaims the approach of day during the darkness of the night. She is represented as mounted on a chariot, and covered with a veil bespangled with stars. The <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a> generally went before her as her constant messengers. Sometimes she is seen holding under her arms two children, one of which is black, representing Death, and the other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, representing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SLEEP">Sleep</a>. Some of the poets have described her as a woman veiled in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>, crowned with poppies, and on a chariot drawn by owls and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BATS">bats</a>. (See <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>, Theog.; <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>, Orestes and Ion; also Pausanias.)

NOY

Pages 355-355

Sir William, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a>, whose conduct was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> causes of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> in England, was born in 1577. During the former <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a> his sentiments were patriotic, and he was distinguished in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a> as one of the most formidable opponents of the despotism of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. No sooner, however, had he been appointed attorney-general in 1631, than he was suddenly transformed into one of the most pliant tools of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a>. The legal knowledge and ingenuity of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> apostate began to be employed in extorting from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> certain precedents which might countenance the tyranny of his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. He consummated his treachery to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> by devising the project of levying ship-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. But before he had seen the disasters which that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of his contributed to bring upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, he died, in 1634. Among his valuable legal works are, A Treatise of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">Principal</a> Grounds and Maxims of the Laws of England, of which the seventh edition was published in 12mo, 1806; and The Compleat Lawyer, of which the latest edition was published in 8vo, 1674.

NUBIA

Pages 355-357

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, lying between <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> on the N. and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a> on the S., the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> on the E. and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">Desert</a> on the W.; and extending from N. Lat. 11. to 24., E. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 25. to 36. The name, however, is not always applied to the whole of this region, but is restricted by some geographers to the country east of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, while the natives themselves apply the terms Nooba, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Wady-el-Nooba, to a comparatively small por- The aspect of the country in Lower Nubia is very different from that of Egypt, though both alike form <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the valley of the Nile. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which consist chiefly of sandstone and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, approach much nearer to the river, leaving only a narrow strip of arable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>'s edge; and the rocks in some places extend into the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the river, forming rapids, the lowest of which, called the First Cataract, occurs at the confines of Egypt and Nubia. Beyond the hills which line the river on either side stretches the desert of Nubia, extending on the one side to the Red Sea, and on the other being separated from the Sahara only by inconsiderable hills and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-lands. In some places the desert comes quite <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the Nile, forming <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> banks to the river, and in other places the banks are covered only with a thin strip of vegetation. Upper Nubia occupies the lowest of the three table-lands which are supposed to constitute this part of the African continent. The elevation increases towards the southern border of Nubia, which has a height of 4000 feet above the sea. This district is also occupied by several mountain chains, which do not for the most part, as in Egypt, extend <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the river, but from west to east, forming numerous valleys in the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. Of these chains the most important are the Gebel Saigre, Gebel Safiata, and Orbay Langay; the last of which stretches from Faka on the Albana to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUAKIN">Suakin</a> on the Red Sea, and has numerous offshoots in the eastern Nubian desert. A range of mountains stretches along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Red Sea, but these are not very <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, nor in any way remarkable. Coarse grey granite, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-QUARTZ">quartz</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MICA">mica</a>-slate are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> geological formations of Upper Nubia. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> and silver <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> are said to exist near the shores of the Red Sea; but all the attempts made by the Pasha of Egypt to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> them have proved fruitless. In Upper Nubia the Nile is not so closely shut in by mountains as in the lower region; and this country is also watered by other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, which discharge their waters into it. At the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> Cataract immense plains stretch out from either margin of the stream, exhibiting, it is said, even in their present neglected condition, unequivocal indications of fertility; and as there seems to be little doubt that in former ages the annual inundation extended considerably beyond the limits of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> cultivation, so it may reasonably be presumed that anciently the country was much more productive and populous than in modern times, when the decrease of the inundation, and the continual encroachment of the moving sands of the desert on either side, have combined to produce the desolation which now prevails. At present the Nile seldom or never overflows its banks in this part of Nubia; and the portion of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> cultivated is irrigated by means of sakkeas, or Persian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> constructed for raising the water of the river to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the adjacent ground. The eastern <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Nile is much better adapted for cultivation than the western, being more easily irrigated by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> means. But it is not a little remarkable, that all the splendid ruins for which this region is distinguished, and which exhibit so great labour, ingenuity, and skill, are found upon the opposite bank; a circumstance which seems to strengthen the presumption that Nubia was formerly much more fertile and populous than in the present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The country on the banks of the Nile is composed of two parts,—Wady Kenoos and Wady Nooha, so called from the tribes who inhabit them, and who differ from each other in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The former extends from the confines of Egypt on the south to Wady Sebooa; and the latter, from which the general name of the country appears to have been derived, stretches as far as the frontier of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DONGOLA">Dongola</a>. The chief distinction between these two parts consists in the circumstance, that the languages spoken in each are entirely different. The grain which forms the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object of Nubian cultivation is dhourra, the *Andropogon sorghum* of botanists. It is raised upon the patches of soil irrigated by means of the sakkeas or Persian wheels, of which there are from 600 to 700 between the First and Second Cataracts; and, when ground, it is formed into a cake somewhat resembling the Abyssinian *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEFF">teff</a>*. After the dhourra, the Nubians raise a crop of barley, French beans, lentils, and sometimes also of water-melons. Sometimes a third crop is raised in the year, and this in these <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> generally consists of dhourra again. <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a> is everywhere cultivated, and constitutes the principal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> of all classes, being either smoked or sucked in a peculiar manner between the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> and the lip. Animal food is scarce, and seldom eaten, even by the chiefs or sheiks. The liquors used are palm-wine, a spirit distilled from dates, and a sort of beer called *booza*, which is made from dhourra. Excessive <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> in these liquors is general throughout the whole country. The only fruit trees cultivated in Nubia are palms, but the soil is adapted for several others. Great sameness prevails in the vegetation of the desert, the trees being mostly <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACACIAS">acacias</a>, tamarisks, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> and doum palms. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Nubia, though intensely hot in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, is nevertheless remarkably healthy. This is no doubt a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> dryness of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, occasioned by the absence of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> and the absorbent qualities of the soil. The upper regions of Nubia, however, are by no means destitute of rain, but are exposed from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> to May to those showers which cause the overflowing of the Nile. They do not extend N. of 17° 30' N. Lat. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> has seldom or never reached Wady Halfa, and beyond the Second Cataract it is entirely unknown. The small-pox, however, is a fearful scourge, and, owing to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and filthiness of the people, occasionally commits dreadful ravages. The people are now generally known by the name of Nubians, and are called by the Arabs *Barabra*. They consist of the Kenoos and Nooha tribes, and differ considerably in appearance at different places, those to the south being much darker than the inhabitants of the country bordering on Egypt. They are generally well made, strong, and muscular, and have tolerably good features. The women are not handsome, but perfectly well formed, and in general remarkable for agreeable countenances and pleasing manners. Great numbers of the Nubians repair to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, where they usually <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> as porters, and are esteemed for their honesty; but they always return to their native villages with the little <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> which they have saved in plying their humble vocation. They excel the Egyptians in honesty and veracity, though they are inferior in acuteness. They are likewise distinguished for their brave, independent, and patriotic spirit. The inhabitants of Derr-el-Mahas and the more southerly districts differ considerably from the other Nubian tribes. They are of Arab <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, and speak the language and follow the wandering <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of that people. Previously to 1821 the Nubians were independent, being ruled by chiefs of their own; but in that year they were brought under the power of the Egyptian pashas; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Nubia is now, like that of Egypt, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> despotism. Some trade is carried on in Nubia, Sennaar and Shendy being the principal mart for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of eastern Africa. The principal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of export to Egypt are dates, which are obtained here of an excellent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; gold, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, ebony, and slaves are imported into Nubia from the interior of Africa, and thence sent to Egypt, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, or the East; and the principal imports through Egypt are <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, beads, coral, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and hardware. One of the most remarkable features of this region consists in the magnificent monumental remains with which it is covered along the line of the stream, and which continue to perpetuate the genius and power of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the country situated on the Upper Nile. The principal remains in Nubia, beginning with the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the river and proceeding upwards, are the following:—At Dabod on the W. bank, 15 miles above the First Cataract, are the remains of a temple, dedicated, according to a Greek inscription over the entrance, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> Philometer and his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Cleopatra, to Isis and other deities. The temple of Kalabishieh, whose ruins stand on the same side of the Nile, about 29 miles above Dabod, is the largest in Nubia. It does not seem to be earlier than the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Augustus, though the materials have apparently been taken from an older <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. The body of the temple consists of three parts, and has twelve columns in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a>. It stands in the middle of an inclosure, which is entered by a portico with two pyramidal towers. At the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is an ancient temple of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the Pharaohs, cut out of the rock, and adorned with elegant sculptures. The temple of Dendoor, which stands <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> within the tropic, is believed to have been founded by Augustus in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, Isis, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HORUS">Horus</a>. At Dakkleh, further up than Dendoor, are the remains of a temple founded by Ergamun, an Ethiopian <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a> of the age of Ptolemy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>. On the opposite side there are extensive brick ruins, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the names of Remeses VII. and VIII., who lived in the twelfth century B.C. The ruined structure at Saboos has before it a propylon, with two pyramidal towers. The pronaos on each of its longest sides has five columns without capitals, and in front of each is a colossal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, 16 feet in height, with the arms crossed on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, and the usual emblems in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. In front of the propylon are two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, 10 feet in height, with their faces towards the river, and attached by the backs to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> pillars of equal elevation; and an avenue of sixteen sphinxes leads from the bank of the Nile to the temple. The whole fabric appears to be of the remotest antiquity, and is ascribed to the age of Remeses the Great (1355-1289 B.C.). Of the same era is the temple of Derr, which, has some bold though defaced sculptures. But of all the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> of Nubia, that of Abou-Simbel Ebsamboul or Ipsamboul, about 40 miles below the Second Cataract, is incomparably the most remarkable. It has the finest colossal figures of any in Egypt, which, notwithstanding their great size, have countenances of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, when seen from a proper distance. The great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a> contains eight pillars with colossal figures attached to them, and there are many other apartments opening into it. Both the pillars and the walls are covered with representations of battles, storming of castles, triumphs, and sacrifices, in a style, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not superior to, at least bolder than, that of almost any in Egypt, both in regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> and the workmanship. The second hall, which is of less dimensions, contains four pillars about 4 feet <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and the walls are covered with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a> in tolerable preservation. Beyond this there is a chamber of the same width, but shorter, in which is the entrance to the sanctuary; and at each end is a door leading into smaller apartments in the same direction with the adyton. The sanctuary itself is 23 feet in length by 12 in breadth, and contains a pedestal in the centre, with four colossal figures in a sitting posture at the end, all in good order and uninjured. The outside or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> front of this temple is truly magnificent, being 117 feet in width, and 86 feet in height, whilst the space from the top of the cornice to that of the door is 66½ feet, and the height of the door itself 20 feet. There are four enormous sitting figures, the largest in Nubia, or even in Egypt, excepting only the great sphinx at the Pyramids, to which they approach in the proportion of nearly two-thirds. On the top of the door is a statue of Osiris, 20 feet in height, with a colossal figure on each side looking towards it. The cornice of the temple is adorned with hieroglyphics, and under it are a torus and frieze, the one 6 and the other 4 feet in breadth. Above the cornice is a row of squatted monkeys, twenty in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and each 8½ feet across the shoulders. This temple was nearly two-thirds buried in the sand till the year 1817, when the sand was cleared away, and an entrance obtained by Belzoni, Irby, Mangles, and Beechey. In several places of the square border which encircles the front of the temple, and also on the buttresses between the colossal figures, are a number of ovals or rings, containing the name and praenomen of Remeses the Great, the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a> whom the Greeks indicate by the name of Sesostris or Sethosis. The temples at Samneh, situated on the western bank of the river, between the twenty-first and twenty-second <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, afford specimens of a more perfect class of structures; intermediate, it would seem, between such excavations as that of Ebsamboul and the magnificent edifices of Karnak and Luxor. That on the eastern bank has a portico and a hall running parallel to it, behind which are three small and one larger chamber; and that on the other side is more elegant, consisting of one chamber surrounded by a corridor of pillars. The first architectural attempt in Nubia probably was General de la Croix's improvement of some hole or cave in the rock; or d'Anville's, even if the country possessed no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> caves for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> by a people possessing the troglodyte habits natural to the inhabitants of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> climate, the mountains themselves would afford facilities for constructing durable habitations. After having got possession of a hole or cave, the next step of these primitive architects would probably be to extend the excavation, to form several chambers separated by the native rock, and when a compartment of larger dimensions was designed, to have square pillars for the support of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>. In the course of time the outer front, with the inner walls and pillars, would receive decorations derived from imitations of the natural forms of the country, and subjects connected with the historical remembrances or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> creed of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. We see abundant <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> in the rock-temples of Nubia to convince us that the order of progression and improvement here indicated was that actually followed in their gradual enlargement and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a>; yet a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> must have elapsed between the rudest excavation in the rock, such as Derr appears to have been in its primitive state, and the highly-finished sculptures of the great temple of Ebsamboul. In fact, "antiquity appears to have begun" long after these primeval architects had commenced their troglodyte labours. But, in surveying the wonders which crowd the banks of the Nile from Meröe to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMPHIS">Memphis</a>, our minds become insensibly impressed with the reflection, that the wealth, power, and genius which produced them have entirely passed away; that, if new worlds have risen, and new races been discovered, "we have lost old nations;" and that, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a> of ages, empires themselves vanish, like the baseless fabric of a vision, leaving scarcely a wreck or trace behind them. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> between what now is and what once must have been in Ethiopia and in Egypt, is indeed most striking; nor is it easy to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, even in thought, through the various scenes of conquest and desolation which must have conspired to produce the effects we contemplate. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> sheds no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on events and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> which the lapse of 3000 years has covered with impenetrable obscurity; and whilst groping our way amidst temples dedicated to gods, and structures raised in honour of heroes, whose very names <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> like voices from the dead, we content ourselves with the conclusion, which all the monuments impress on us, that long before the dawn of history there had existed in that singular region a great people, whose architectural monuments have outlasted their learning, their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and almost even their very name.

NUDDA

Pages 357-358

a district of British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, under the lieu- Nuddea tenant-governor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, comprised within the delta of the Ganges, and lying between Lat. 22. 49. and 24. 10. N., and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 88. 9. and 89. 11. E. It is about 90 miles in length from N. to S., by 45 in breadth, and has an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 2942 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is well watered and highly fertile, producing in abundance <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, millet, maize, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-seeds, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. Pop. 298,736. Nuddea, a town of British India, in the district of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURDWAN">Burdwan</a>, at the commencement of the Hooghly River, 80 miles N. of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a>. Lat. 23. 25. N., Long. 88. 22. E. It was the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a Hindu principality anterior to the Mogul conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, and was taken and entirely destroyed in 1204. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times it has been the seat of a Brahmin seminary of learning; anterior, however, to that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENARES">Benares</a>. Nugeneah, a town of British India, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Rohilkund, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a>-West Provinces, in Lat. 29. 27. N., Long. 78. 30. E. It is noted for its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of fire-arms; and contains about 14,000 inhabitants. Nuisance, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Nusance, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a thing done to the annoyance of another. Nuisances are either public or private. A public or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> nuisance is an offence against the public in general, either by doing what tends to the annoyance of all the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a>'s subjects, or by neglecting to do what the common good requires; in which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a>, all annoyances and injuries to streets, highways, bridges, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, as also disorderly ale-houses, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>-houses, and the like, are held to be common nuisances. A private nuisance is, when only one person or family is annoyed by the doing of anything; as when a person stops up the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of another's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, or builds in such a manner that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> falls from his house upon his neighbour's. In Scotch law, there is no recognised distinction between public and private nuisances. Numa Pompilius, the successor of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> on the throne of Rome, was the son of an illustrious Sabine, and was raised to the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> by the unanimous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and people. After a remarkably popular reign of 42 years, during which he endeared himself both to his own people and to the surrounding nations by his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abilities and singular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, Numa died in the year of Rome 82. (See <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>.) Numantia, a very noble <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the ornament of the Hither <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and celebrated for the long <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> of 20 years which it maintained against the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. The inhabitants obtained some advantage over the Roman forces, till Scipio Africanus was empowered to finish the war, and to effect the destruction of Numantia. The town occupied an eminence of great steepness, and was approachable only on one side. Scipio began the siege with an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 60,000 men, and was bravely opposed by the besieged, who were no more than 4000 men able to bear arms. They held out against the enemy with the most indomitable courage while their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> lasted; but being reduced to desperation, they set fire to their houses, and destroyed themselves, so that not even one remained to adorn the triumph of the conqueror. It was taken by the Romans 134 B.C., and the conqueror obtained the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Numanticus. It is conjectured that the modern Puente de Garay, near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SORIA">Soria</a>, marks the site nearly of this once famous city. Fragments of antiquity are occasionally dug up there. (Accounts of this memorable siege are to be found in Appian, B. Hisp. 48, &c.; Eutropius, iv.; Cicero, De Off.; Strabo, iii.; also in the Compendio Historiae, b. iii., of Pedro <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TUTOR">Tutor</a> y Melo, Soria, 1690.) Numbers, Book of. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>. Numerals. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>. Numarianus, Marcus Aurelius, a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, succeeded to the purple conjointly with his elder <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Carinus, on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CARUS">Carus</a>, A.D. 284, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>, and was murdered in the same year, after a reign of eight months. (See Roman History.) Numidia, an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, which owed its name to the circumstance that its early inhabitants were pastoral tribes (Numides). These tribes, differing both in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> and character, extended their wanderings from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> as far west as the Fortunate <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>. The limits of the country were therefore for a long <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> very ill-defined. It was not until the time of the Punic wars that the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Numidians came to be definitely restricted to the Massylii and the Massylli, who dwelt between the River Mulucha (Malouia) on the W., and the Carthaginian territory on the E., and were divided from each other by the River Ampsaga (Wad-el-Kebir). These two tribes were then athletic and warlike savages, living on the sides of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in little huts called magalia, and scouring the plains on horseback without saddle or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a>. From that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, however, the character of the people, and the condition of the country, began to be changed by foreign interference and the events of war. During the struggle between <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> and the Romans, Syphax, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the Massylii, espoused the cause of the former, and Masinissa, the prince of the Massylli, espoused the cause of the latter. Syphax was defeated, along with his great ally, in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Zama, B.C. 202; his territories were incorporated with those of the Massylli; all the Carthaginian district, with the exception of a portion around the capital city, was added; and Masinissa received possession of the whole, with the title of King of Numidia. It then became the aim of that able prince to civilize his people by the introduction of arts and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. After his death in 148 B.C., the same line of policy was followed, with even more success, by his son and successor Micipsa. But the commotions that broke out in the ensuing reign marred the prosperity which a long peace had been fostering. Jugurtha, the nephew, and Adherbal and Hiempsal, the sons of Micipsa, were left <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>-heirs to the throne. The first of these princes was unscrupulous and ambitious, and did not rest until he had defeated and murdered his cousins, and had seized the sceptre of the entire <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. This involved the Numidians in a contest with the Romans. After all the wiles of intrigue and the stratagems of war had proved unsuccessful, the usurper was captured and put to death in 106 B.C., and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> was bestowed upon Hiempsal II. But the disasters of Numidia were not yet ended. Juba I., the son and successor of the last-mentioned prince, espoused the cause of Pompey during the Roman civil war. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> defeat of his party at the battle of Thapsus, in 46 B.C., left him exposed to the vengeance of Caesar. The desperate state of his affairs drove him to commit <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUICIDE">suicide</a>; and his kingdom, reduced into the form of a Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, was placed under the governorship of Sallust the historian. Soon after this period Numidia began to enter upon a long period of prosperity. The "jus coloniae" was conferred upon its capital, Cirta (Constantina), and upon its other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>—Rusicade, Hippo-Regius (<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BONA">Bona</a>), Sicca (Kef), Lambasa, and Theveste. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a> was diffused by means of the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>; peace was preserved by means of the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>; and the wild Numidian horsemen were thus transformed in course of time into a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of industrious peasants. The gospel found an easy entrance, and prospered so rapidly, that the country is said to have contained in the fifth century no fewer than 123 episcopal sees. It was not until the invasion of the Saracens, in the seventh century, that the prosperity of Numidia, simultaneously with its Christianity, received a fatal blow. (See Algiers. For further information regarding Numidian history, see also Masinissa, Micipsa, Jugurtha, and Juba I.)

NUMISMATICS

Pages 358-378

INTRODUCTION. The science of Numismatics treats of coins and medals. It acquaints us with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-METALS">metals</a> used in their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, their various <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> and devices, their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> execution and artistic merit. It tells us of the different denominations of coins, with their relation to one another, and the laws by which they were regulated. The earliest known coins were issued by the Greeks, most probably in the eighth century before the Christian era. By the fourth century the whole civilized world used <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, each state generally having its proper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COINAGE">coinage</a>. This has <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> to the present <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>; so that now there are few nations without a metal currency of their own, and of these but a small proportion are wholly unacquainted with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of coins. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of varieties of coins and medals of which specimens are preserved in collections may be estimated at not less than 200,000, and future discoveries <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably greatly raise this sum. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of monuments of such length and completeness affords, as might be expected, very important illustration to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and to kindred branches of knowledge. This is, indeed, the real value of Numismatics; and the student will do well to keep it constantly before him, for thus he will be saved from the narrow view of a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> collector, by which many have been led in a false <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and so discredit has been brought upon the science. Coins, although they confirm history, rarely correct it, and never very greatly. The earliest belong to a time and to nations as to which we are not otherwise wholly ignorant, and they do not afford us that precise information that would fill in any important details of the meagre sketch of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> history. We <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> from them scarcely any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> historical information, except that certain cities <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> princes issued money. When, in later times, the devices and inscriptions of the coins give more detailed information, history is far fuller and clearer, so that the numismatic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> is rarely more than corroborative. There are, indeed, some remarkable exceptions to this rule, as in the case of the Bactrian coins, which have supplied the outlines of a portion of history which was otherwise almost wholly lost. The value of the corroborative evidence afforded by coins must not, however, be overlooked. It chiefly relates to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, although it also adds to our knowledge of the pedigrees of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> houses.
