Here, too, he conceived the idea of his Correggio, the first and best of the long line of art-dramas in which Germany has since been prolific, although it was in Parma that this fine work fitly took a definite shape, which was afterwards perfected in Rome. After an absence of five years, Oehlenschläger returned in 1810 to Copenhagen, where he was already famous, and an enthusiastic reception awaited him. He had endowed some of the finest national legends with a noble dramatic life, and laid the foundation of a national drama of the best kind. His countrymen were proud of him, and at this early period, as through all the rest of his long life, were not sparing in their demonstrations of regard. He was appointed professor of aesthetics at the university of Copenhagen,—a position which he continued to fill with honour till nearly the close of his life. On the 10th of May 1810 he married Christiana Heger, to whom he had been so long betrothed, and whom, after the companionship of many years of uninterrupted happiness, he lived to regret. From the time of his return to Copenhagen, Oehlenschläger's life was one unbroken career of literary labour and of literary honour. He wrote much in nearly all departments of the belles lettres,—poems, dramas (serious and comic), operettas, tales, and novels. It is by his dramas, however, that posterity will know him. Besides comedies and operas, he wrote twenty-four tragedies, of which nineteen are on Scandinavian themes. These are of various and unequal merit; but all are more or less deserving of perusal, and some will rank among the first in the first class of modern dramas. Like all dramatists of the highest order, Oehlenschläger himself is not seen in the best of his works. His characters feel and speak with a spontaneousness, and truth to the situation, which make the reader forget the author in the living reality of the scene. The art to blot, however, was one which Oehlenschläger seems never to have learned. As the first impulse came, so he wrote; and his writings accordingly bear many traces of feebleness, which a more vigorous judgment would have been at pains to remove. Oehlenschläger was scarcely less esteemed in Sweden than in Denmark. In the summer of 1829 he visited that country, where he was greeted by all classes with a burst of enthusiasm such as commonly is bestowed only on conquerors or kings. He was met on the high road by a procession of students. Addresses were presented to him from all quarters. At the distribution of degrees in the ancient cathedral of Lund, Bishop Tegner, the greatest poet of Sweden, saluted him with a panegyric in hexameters in which he was hailed as the king of the poets of the north, and placed a laurel crown upon his head amidst a storm of music and artillery. Soon afterwards he was made a knight of the North Star by the King of Sweden, and received the diploma of doctor of philosophy from the university of Lund. Ovations not less gratifying awaited him on a subsequent visit to Sweden, and also to Norway. In 1813 he received from the King of Denmark the knighthood of Dannebrog, and in 1839 he was appointed counsellor of state. Other and higher honours were subsequently conferred upon him in his own country; and from the sovereigns of Sweden, Prussia, and Belgium he received similar distinctions. A great festival was held at Copenhagen on the 14th November 1849, in honour of his seventieth birthday, on which occasion he recited a poetical address, in which he said, "Although the end far distant may not be, There's life and sinew in the old man yet; To you I drink, and drain the cup with glee, For 'tis no funeral feast that here is set." He was then in the full enjoyment of all his powers, and was even then busy with literary tasks. But about six weeks afterwards symptoms of a breaking up of the constitution appeared; and he died on the 20th of January 1850. About an hour and a half before his death he requested his son to read to him that part of the scene in the fifth act of his tragedy of Socrates, where the philosopher speaks of death. "It is," he said, "so unspeakably beautiful." He heard the passage read with deep emotion, "and with a smile," says the biographer, "of rapturous delight." When it was concluded, he put an end to the reading, and took leave of his family. The incident is characteristic, not as has been said, of the poet's vanity, but of his simple faith, which regarded himself only as the medium through which an inspiration from a higher source spoke. So it was with Oehlenschläger through life. His poetry flowed from him under an inspiration as unconscious, and often as fitful, as music from the wind-swept chords of an Æolian lyre. When the mood passed, he seems to have rarely set himself to the task of rejecting what was weak or indifferent, or heightening by the touches of art what had been left imperfect in the heat of composition. Oehlenschläger's death was felt as a national loss, and his obsequies were celebrated with almost regal honours. A funeral oration was pronounced over his remains by the Bishop of Seeland in the cathedral of Copenhagen, and they were then borne to the church of Fredericksborg attended by a crowd of more than 20,000 people, or about a sixth of the entire population of the capital. The prince royal, the royal aides-de-camp, the whole diplomatic body, all the clergy, and the different guilds of arts and manufactures, swelled the train; and the coffin was borne by the youth of the public schools. Thus royally attended, the great Scandinavian bard was laid to rest in the grave of his fathers on the 26th January 1850. Oehlenschläger was robust in body as in mind,—a burly man, with a large head, and features which beamed with intelligence and vivacity. He seemed to be rather a child of the sunny south than of the north. His complexion was tinged with ruddy bronze, his eyes were dark and brilliant, his smile full and joyous, his gestures animated and quick. His sensibilities were at all times readily moved. He enjoyed keenly, and his sympathies were wide and genial. There was to the last much of the child in him; and in the midst of their admiration his friends were often moved to smile at his harmless egotism. Rarely has a poet's life been happier, or more in harmony with his nature. Born poor, he was fortunate in the love of parents with whom he grew up in an atmosphere of simplicity, integrity, and piety. He was fortunately enabled by well-timed patronage to follow from the first the instincts of his genius. His country early recognised his claims. Placed by it in a position to pursue his literary career without anxiety, he was cheered through life by the assurance that his efforts were watched with interest, and welcomed with hearty sympathy. Rich in purse he never was; but he was rich in the love of a wife to whom he was devoted, and of children who caused him no regrets,—rich in the possession of all his powers of mind and body to the close of a long life,—rich in the love of honoured friends, and in the admiration of his country. In him genius was happily allied with goodness; and the world dealt kindly with the man whom nature had endowed with many of her choicest gifts. (π. m.—n.)

OELS

Pages 496-496

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a>, on the Oelsa, 17 miles N.N.E. of Breslau. It is fortified; and has an extensive ducal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> built in the form of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and containing a good library; a Roman Catholic and three Protestant churches, a synagogue, several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a> of woollen, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and silken stuffs are carried on here; and there are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>. Pop. 6928. OENIADÆ (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Trikardho), an important town of Arcamania in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, was situated on the western <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Achelous (Aspropotamo), about 2 miles from the mouth of that river. Its name was probably derived from Æneus, a legendary Ætolian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERO">hero</a>. It stood on an insulated hill, strengthened by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> walls, and surrounded on all sides by extensive morasses. These fortifications, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, rendered the town for a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> a formidable and invincible foe to the Athenians. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a> was unable to take it by siege in Oenotria 454 B.C.; Phormion advanced against it in 429 B.C., but could not <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> across the swamps; and it was not until 424 B.C. that it was forced by the general <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a> to take the Athenian side in the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>. This seems to have been a fatal blow to the independence of Oeniadæ. In the latter half of the fourth century B.C. it was taken by the Ætolians; in 219 B.C. it passed into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>; and in 211 B.C. it was captured by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and given once more to the Ætolians. Although the citizens were freed from the domination of their fellow-countrymen in 189 B.C., they never recovered their former importance. From that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> Oeniadæ disappeared from the arena of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">Large</a> portions of its walls still remain in excellent preservation. OENOTRIA: See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">ITALY</a>.

OESSEL

Pages 496-496

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> belonging to Russia, stretches across the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGA">Riga</a>, between N. Lat. 58. and 58. 40., E. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 21. 40. and 23. 20. Its length from S. by W. to N. by E. is about 45 miles; <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> breadth, 12 miles; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>, about 1200 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. Next to <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, this is the largest of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Baltic. It has steep and bold coasts, and a rocky undulating surface, watered by numerous streams. The rocks are for the most <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> calcareous; and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, though not naturally fertile, may be made productive by means of manure. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of the island is covered with forests, and a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of it is used as pasture ground. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is milder in winter than that of the adjacent mainland; but in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and autumn severe storms frequently occur. Corn is raised in sufficient quantities to furnish an article of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>; wheat, rye, barley, and oats being the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> crops; while <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> are also cultivated. Many of the inhabitants are also employed in pastoral and piscatorial pursuits. Few <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are carried on. The majority of the people are Lutherans; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARENSBURG">Arensburg</a>, on the S.E. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. Oesel at one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> belonged to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEUTONIC">Teutonic</a> knights, but was seized by the Danes at an early <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and ceded by them to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> in 1645. In the beginning of the eighteenth century it was taken possession of by Russia, to which power it was finally ceded in 1721 along with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, of which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> it forms a part. Pop. about 40,000.

OETINGER

Pages 496-496

FRIEDRICH CHRISTOPH, a mystic divine, was born in 1702 at Göppingen in Württemberg. After finishing his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the university of Leipzig, and occupying himself with several learned engagements, he was appointed pastor at Hirschau in 1738. It was about this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> that he began to imbibe the doctrines of mysticism from the treatises of Boehmen and others. In 1765 his edition of the works of Swedenborg, in 2 vols. 8vo, and his treatise entitled Earthly and Heavenly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, revealed his opinions to the public, and drew <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon him the reprehension of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> superiors. Yet protected by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Württemberg, and aided by his own excellent character, he rose to a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> position in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. After passing through several grades of promotion, he was appointed prelate at Murhard, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> there till his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1782.

OFANTO

Pages 496-496

a river of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">Kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, rises in the Apennines, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Principato Ultra, flows E.N.E., separating <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPITANATA">Capitanata</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BASILICATA">Basilicata</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, and falls into the Adriatic, after a course of 75 miles. On the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> is the field of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Cannae, where the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were totally defeated by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>, n.c. 216.

OFFENBACH

Pages 496-500

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>-Darmstadt, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Starkenburg, on the left banks of the Main, here crossed by a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of boats, 5 miles E.S.E. of Frankfort. It is well Offenburg built and partly walled; and has a ducal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, several churches, a school, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>-houses, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, &c. Its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are extensive, consisting of woollen, cotton, and silken fabrics; gloves, wax-cloth, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, earthenware, &c. There are no fewer than ninety-five manufacturing establishments in the town, employing 6000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and producing annually about L650,000 worth of goods. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is also remarkable for its bookbinding, in which art it is superior to any other place in Germany. An <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> trade is carried on in wine and other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. Pop. (1852) 13,087. Offenburg, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BADEN">Baden</a>, in the circle of Mittelrhein, on a hill near the Kinzig, 42 miles S.S.W. of Karlsruhe. It has a town-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>' <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, school, nunnery, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, &c. Manufactures of leather, glass, and other articles, and some trade, are carried on. Pop. 4010. Officinal, is the name applied to such medicines, whether simple <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, as are required to be constantly kept in the apothecaries' shops. Ogdensburg, a town of the United States of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, state of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORK">York</a>, on a plain at the confluence of the Oswegatchie with the St Lawrence, 200 miles N.N.W. of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALBANY">Albany</a>. It is well and regularly built; and contains numerous churches, belonging to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>, Episcopalians, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>, Baptists, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>; an academy; and three banks. There are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-foundries, machine-shops, and other manufactories. The trade of the town is considerable; and it communicates by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>-vessels with the different ports on Lake <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ONTARIO">Ontario</a>. It is also connected by railway with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOSTON">Boston</a> and New York. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of vessels that entered the port in 1852 was 830; tonnage, 347,698; that cleared, 798; tonnage, 341,188. Pop. (1853) about 6500. Ogechee, a river of the United States of North America, state of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, flows S.E., and falls into the Atlantic by Ossahaw <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>, 20 miles S. of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAVANNAH">Savannah</a>. Its whole length is 250 miles; and it is navigable by sloops for 30 or 40 miles. Ogilvy, John, an industrious author and literary speculator, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in 1600. His father was a prisoner for debt in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BENCH">Bench</a>, and could give him but little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. Yet the boy had a practical ingenuity, and an ever-wakeful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> which led him over the greatest difficulties on towards success. While supporting himself by teaching <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> to the families of the English <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, he contrived to gratify his eager avidity for learning. In 1649 his literary accomplishments had become so considerable that he became an author by profession, and began to publish a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of metrical translations of some of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> classics. His <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> appeared in that same year, his Fables of Aesop in 1651, his Iliad in 1650, and his Odyssey in 1665. Yet although Ogilvy had gained distinction by these publications, and although he had been appointed superintendent of the poetical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the coronation pageantry in 1661, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the revels in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> in 1662, he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be the same plodding and practical <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> of business. After the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fire of 1666 had reduced him to beggary, he contrived in a short <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> to set up a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-press; and in the capacity of cosmographer to the king, published a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATLAS">atlas</a> in several folio volumes, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> in England from his own actual survey. His <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> took place in 1676. Ohio, one of the United States of North America, situated on the river of the same name, which separates it on the S. and S.E. from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KENTUCKY">Kentucky</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>; on the E. it has <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>; N., <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">Lakes</a> Erie and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MICHIGAN">Michigan</a>; and on the W., <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIANA">Indiana</a>. It has an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 39,961 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, being somewhat greater than that of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>; and, in all respects, it is one of the most important states of the valley of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a> or of the American Union. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is delightfully varied, and presents a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> from 600 to 1000 feet above the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. A ridge of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> lands divides the waters flowing north into Lake Erie from those flowing south into the aspect Ohio. There is a ridge crossing the state in the latitude of Columbus, south of which the surface is diversified by hills and valleys. Swamps and morasses occasionally occur, forming, however, only a twentieth part of the whole surface. The river-bottoms are extensive and very fertile. Prairies are numerous; but the country was originally covered with magnificent forests, which are still far from being extinct. The Ohio River and Lake Erie receive the waters of the state. Those streams which enter into the Ohio are the Muskingum, Hockhocking, Scioto, Miami, &c. The Muskingum is navigable 75 miles for steamers, and for small boats nearly to its source. The Hockhocking courses through a hilly and beautiful country, and is a deep and narrow stream. The Scioto can be ascended to nearly its source, and has many thriving <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on its banks. Its valley is wide and fertile. The Little Miami is less adapted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> than to mill-sites. The Big Miami enters the Ohio in the S.W. corner of the state, after a course of 100 miles. The northern <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Maumee, Sandusky, Cuyahoga, which are in part navigable, but furnish the most abundant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>-power for manufacturing purposes. The other streams are the Portage, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>, Rocky, Vermillion, &c. Over nearly the entire surface of the state there lies a deposit of various thickness, known by the name of alluvium, believed to have been made by currents of water. One of the most important <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> is a transition <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to the mountain limestone of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It crops out in places, forming, at small cost, a valuable <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> material. East of the Huron and Olantangy rivers the lime stratum dips under one of shale or clay-slats; farther east this passes under a stratum of sandstone; still farther, the sandstone is overlaid by a conglomerate, and then by the lower coal series; and, finally, the upper coal series passes beyond the eastern and south-eastern boundary of the state. One-third of Ohio is therefore within the great coal basin, of which Wheeling, Virginia, is the centre. In several of the southern counties are extensive beds of the best iron. In Western Ohio are found gypsum, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. It is estimated that the beds of workable coal would be sufficient to last 10,000 years, supposing Ohio to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> as much as is now used in England and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. By the census of 1850, it appears that Ohio produced as follows: | Establishments | <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">Capital</a> | Value of products | |---------------|---------|------------------| | Pig iron | 35 | L313,123 | L261,632 | | Iron castings | 183 | 429,923 | 639,444 | | Wrought iron | 6 | 34,331 | 28,632 | | Salt | 32 | 39,320 | 27,558 | The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Tuscarawas is 550 square miles in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and in every part of it, it is said, coal may be found. Professor Mather, in his report on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-GEOLOGY">geology</a> of the state, estimates the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of coal in this county alone at 80,000 millions of bushels! In 1840 the production of coal in Ohio is stated at 2,382,368 bushels, in 1848 at 6,538,968, in 1857 at 40,000,000 bushels; and the production of iron has swelled to the aggregate of 100,000 tons. The coal is bituminous. A belt of ironstone, averaging 12 miles in width, is 100 miles or more in length. Salt <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> are numerous, and salt-works are frequent and successful. Marble, freestone, and gypsum occur. Ohio is noted for the fertility of its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. Where the transition lime rock is the upper stratum, as it is in nearly half the state, the soil is remarkably adapted to wheat and grass; and, indeed, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>-eighths of the state are considered well adapted to the growth of wheat. What is known as the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONNECTICUT">Connecticut</a> Reserve, having a shale and sandstone basis, is less fertile, yet producing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and grains suitable to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. About 25,000,000 acres of land in the state could be brought into cultivation, and would support many millions of inhabitants. On account of its elevation, the climate of Ohio is several degrees lower in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> temperature than on the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> in the Atlantic states. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> is subject to tornadoes, but the autumn is always serene and pleasant, though the winters are occasionally severe. Along the valley of the Ohio the temperature is milder than in the interior, but fever and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGUE">ague</a> prevail to some extent in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a>. The climate otherwise is very healthy,—as much so as that of the majority of the states. In the forests are found black walnut, oak, hickory, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> and other maple, beech, poplar, ash, sycamore, pawpaw, buckeye, cherry, dogwood, elm, hornbeam. The cypress is almost the only evergreen, and it is but scanty. Medicinal roots, such as ginseng, valerian, columbo, snake-root, blood-root, &c., are found. Fish and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> are abundant. At the last federal census (1850), it appeared that there were in Ohio 143,807 farms, having under cultivation about 10,000,000 of acres, with about 8,000,000 more inclosed, but unimproved. The average number of acres to each <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARM">farm</a> was 125; average value of farm, L.518; and of farming implements, L.37. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GROSS">Gross</a> value of all the farms in the state, with their implements and machinery, L.77,500,000. The number of horses, asses, and mules, was 466,820; milch cows, 544,490; working oxen, 65,381; sheep, 3,942,929; and swine, 1,964,770. The total value of live stock was L.9,192,027; of animals slaughtered, L.1,549,839. The quantity of wheat raised was 14,487,351 bushels; of rye, 423,918; oats, 13,472,000; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn, 59,078,695; potatoes, 5,245,760; barley, 212,440; buck-wheat, 638,060; hay, 1,443,142 tons; maple sugar, 4,588,000 lb.; <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, 10,454,449; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, 10,196,371; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a> cocoons, 1,552; and wine, 11,524 gallons. Only another of the United States exceeded Ohio in the production of wheat. The other agricultural products are hops; clover and grass seed; pease and beans; market, nursery, and orchard products; <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> seed, flax, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. The produce of the vineyards is large, and commands a market in all parts of the Union. Ohio, in the possession of coal and iron, may be said to have few rivals in capacity as a manufacturing state, when the full fruition of her reasonable hopes are realized. In 1850, she manufactured cotton goods to the value of L.231,462; pig-iron to about the same amount; castings, L.639,353; wrought-iron, L.266,632. She distilled or brewed nearly 100,000 barrels of ale, and 12,000,000 gallons of whisky, &c. The gross <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STATISTICS">statistics</a> of all the manufactures are as follows:—Establishments, 10,622; capital, L.6,045,733; raw material used, L.7,224,586; hands employed, 51,500; <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> paid, L.2,805,758; annual product, L.13,051,507. Ohio being an inland state, must show very low figures in the foreign <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the Union. For the inland or home trade she enjoys advantages on account of her position with reference to the Ohio, the Mississippi, and the lakes, together with her great works of internal improvements, enjoyed by few, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any, of the other states. One of her leading authorities says, at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of 1857, that her production of corn has reached to 90,000,000 bushels, and of wheat to 22,000,000. He estimates the total agricultural, mining, and manufacturing produce of Ohio for that year at L.40,800,000; and says that Ohio is now worth L.200,000,000, and that three-fourths of it have been made out of the profits of labour applied in the industrial pursuits. She exports L.12,500,000 of products, besides enjoying the commerce of her neighbours. The annual statement of commerce, published at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CINCINNATI">Cincinnati</a>, shows that the total produce received at that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in 1856-57 reached L.16,000,444; and that the exports were L.11,800,447. In the city and vicinity 500,000 barrels of whisky are distilled, consuming 8,000,000 bushels of corn and other grain. Number of hogs packed, 344,512. The city is increasing as a wheat, flour, and tobacco mart. Over 500,000 gallons of wine are produced from the vineyards in the vicinity, giving employment to a large number of persons, and producing large returns to capital. The Ohio Canal was completed in 1832, from the Ohio Internal River to Lake Erie, 307 miles. Its branches or feeders improve, —the Columbus branch, 10 miles in length; the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a> branch, 9 miles; the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> to Hocking, a prolongation of the Lancaster, 56 miles; the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-ZANESVILLE">Zanesville</a> branch, of 14 miles, connects the Ohio Canal with the Muskingum improvement, by which another channel is opened to the Ohio River at Marietta; the Walhonding branch is 25 miles in length. The Miami Canal connects Cincinnati with Lake Erie, 270 miles, and was completed in 1832, with several branches. The whole number of miles of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> constructed by the state is 827, at a cost of over L.3,000,000. The other canals, which are private <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">Sandy</a> and Beaver, 76 miles, extending from the Ohio Canal to the Ohio River, at the mouth of the Beaver; the Mahoning Canal, 77 miles. The canals have, however, in part yielded to the railroads, and are in general far from being works of the first class. The oldest railroads are the Little Miami, from Cincinnati to Springfield, 84 miles; the Mad River, from Lake Erie to Springfield, 134 miles; the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a> and Sandusky; the Lake Erie and Kalamazoo, from <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, on Lake Erie, to Adrian, forming a junction with the Michigan Southern <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROAD">Road</a>, to which it forms an outlet to the roads of Ohio, 35 miles. It would occupy too much space, however, to enter into a detail of the numerous railroad routes now in operation in Ohio. They constitute several great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, running through the States from east to west, and from north to south, bringing nearly every county and town in its limits within reach of railroad improvement. Perhaps one of the most important of all these great works is the Ohio and Mississippi Railroad, 330 miles in length, which has been lately completed, and connects by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> route the cities of Cincinnati and St <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>. The railroads in progress or in operation in Ohio, at this time, make up an aggregate length of 3000 miles; the surface of the country being most favourable to their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>. There are no lines of pre-eminent importance, because it is said that trade and commerce are not, as in other states, forced into peculiar channels by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> configuration of the country. Among the cities are Cincinnati, which is known as the City "<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> of the West," supposed now to have a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of over 200,000, making it the fifth city of the American Union; Columbus, the capital of the state, is the centre of a rich country, which is daily adding to its opulence and extent; Dayton is at the meeting of various railroad lines, and is therefore accessible from every point; Zanesville, on the Muskingum, is in the midst of a rich and populous valley region; <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHILLICOTHE">Chillicothe</a>, on the Scioto, is inclosed by picturesque hills; Springfield is at the junction of the Mad River and Lagonda Creek, which affords every variety for mill-sites; Steubenville and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a> are on the Ohio; Sandusky city is on Lake Erie; and Toledo on the Maumee River, at the terminus of the Wabash and Erie Canal. The amount appropriated for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> in Ohio from the Education, several state funds reached, in 1855, L.544,540. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, whole number of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> schools was 12,012; number &c. of scholars attending, 357,547 males, and 311,477 females. Total number of school-houses 7830, which had been erected at a cost of L.464,561. There are 91 high schools, having about 4000 scholars; and 88 schools for coloured children, with about the same number of attendants. There were also a large number of German schools, adapted to that class of population. Twenty-six daily newspapers were printed in 1850, 10 tri-weekly, 201 weekly; total of all classes, 261, printing annually 30,447,407 copies. The total number of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, other than private, was 352, having 186,828 volumes. The whole number of paupers reported was but 1673. There is a lunatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> at Columbus, which had at the last statement 261 inmates. Two other institutions of like character have been opened at Newburg and Dayton. The Ohio <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENITENTIARY">penitentiary</a> at Columbus has about 600 inmates. A library and schools are attached to the prison, and the convicts are instructed in the elementary branches. The state derives a small revenue from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAF_AND_DUMB">deaf and dumb</a> asylum, with 148 occupants; and a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> asylum, containing 72. The value of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> property in Ohio, by the census of 1850, was L2,413,812, and the number of the church sittings was 1,457,769; the Methodist being the predominating <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, giving, with the Baptists, one-half of the whole number of seats. There were, in 1850, 26 colleges, with 3621 pupils; 206 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> and private schools, with 15,052 pupils; 66,020 persons in the state over twenty years of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> were incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-READING">reading</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, or about 3 per cent. of that class, which compares very favourably with other western states. Revenue. The total revenue of the state of Ohio in the year ending with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1856 was L756,492, and the expenditure L731,681. The state cannot, by its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> debt for internal improvement. Total debt in 1856, L3,390,334; value of the real estate at the same time, L120,387,191; and of the personal estate, L58,962,250. Total taxes of all sorts, L1,765,520. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. After the western exploration of Marquette (1673) from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a>, and the expedition of D'Iberville to the mouth of the Mississippi and up its stream, the French began the construction of forts throughout the extensive region which they embraced. Thus was founded their claim to Ohio; whilst the English, on the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, claimed it from grants made by their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, which extended from sea to sea, and from a cession made by the six nations of Indians, who claimed the entire sovereignty of the Ohio valley. The English Ohio <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> having made a settlement on the Great Miami, it was destroyed by the French in 1752, at which time <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> occurring between the two nations, many hostile expeditions were conducted with different results. The defeat of Braddock was followed by the victories of Dunmore. On the return of peace in 1763, the whole of Canada was ceded to England, and with it all the territory to the east of the Mississippi River. After the War of Independence the whole of the western lands held by the several states were ceded to the federal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Surveys and sales of these lands being at once made, the Ohio New England Company purchased a tract lying adjacent to the Scioto and Muskingum rivers, where, in 1788, Marietta was begun, the first permanent settlement in Ohio. Governor <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a> St Clair was appointed territorial governor. In 1787 John <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a> Symmes purchased from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONGRESS">Congress</a> a million of acres in Ohio, northward from the Ohio River, and between the two Miamis, in which region was founded the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> settlement at Columbia, about five miles distant from the present city of Cincinnati. Mathias Denman purchased for 500 dollars the site on which Cincinnati is built, and the first cabin was erected in 1788. Other settlements immediately followed. The Indians, in despite of all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> stipulation, continued to harass the settlers. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BLOCK">Block</a>-houses were constructed; and in 1789 Fort <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WASHINGTON">Washington</a>, as a means of protection, was begun. These aggressions continuing, General Harmer, with 1300 men, marched against the Indian towns, but was compelled to retreat. In 1791 General St Clair, at the head of an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 3000 men, undertaking a similar enterprise, was attacked by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of nearly all the north-western tribes, and after a gallant struggle, sustained a most disastrous defeat. The result of those reverses was severely felt in the settlement, and for some time the tide of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMIGRATION">emigration</a> actually ceased. In 1794 General Wayne assembled an army at Greenville, and soon obtained a decisive victory over a force of 2000 warriors, at the rapids of the Maumee. Not until the country was laid waste, and forts on every hand were seen springing up, did these hardy warriors abandon their futile struggles. "When we consider," says an authority, "the fierce and unrelenting warfare waged by the Indian tribe upon the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a> settlements of the West, during thirty-seven years of almost uninterrupted conflict from 1757, when the first white man was killed in Kentucky, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of Wyne's victory, we may form some faint idea of the toil and perils and sufferings of the bold and hardy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PIONEERS">pioneers</a> who effected the colonization of the Western World. An Indian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, at the conclusion of a treaty yielding up the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of soil in Kentucky, said to Boone,—<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">Brother</a>, we have given you a fine land, but I think you <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> have trouble to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> it;" and his prediction was fully verified there and elsewhere." Constant streams of population began now to pour into Ohio. Connecticut sent many to her reserved tract bordering on Lake Erie. In 1798 the inhabitants of the territory numbered 5000, with eight organized counties. The first meeting of territorial legislature was held in September 1799. William Henry Harrison, then secretary of the territory, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the United States, was at that time elected to Congress. In 1802 the federal government authorized a convention to form a state constitution. It sat at Chillicothe; and Ohio was admitted into the Federal Union soon after. The first legislature met in the same place in 1803; and two years later the United States acquired, by another Indian treaty, the reserve west of the Cuyahoga River, and subsequently the Maumee and Sandusky region. In 1811 the Indians were defeated by General Harrison at Tippecanoe; and in 1816 the seat of government was removed from Chillicothe to Columbus, where it now is. | Population | |------------| | Whites | 1800 | 1810 | 1820 | 1830 | 1840 | 1850 | | Coloured | | | | | | | | Total | 45,335 | 230,700 | 581,434 | 937,903 | 1,519,467 | 1,980,929 | Density to the square <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in 1840, 38-02; 1850, 49-55. Of the total population, but 1,219,452 were born in the state, and 538,134 in the other American states; and 218,512 were born in foreign countries. Of these, about 120,000 were of German origin. Ohio, a river of the United States of North America, is formed by the confluence of the Alleghany and Monongahela, which rise in the Alleghany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, and unite at Pittsburg, in the west of Pennsylvania. It then flows generally towards the S.E., separating the states of Ohio, Indiana, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ILLINOIS">Illinois</a>, on the right, from those of Virginia and Kentucky, on the left; and falls into the Mississippi 1216 miles above its mouth; N. Lat. 37° W. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 89° 10'. Its whole length is more than 950 miles; but its length in a straight line is not more than 614. At the confluence of the two great branches, the Ohio is somewhat more than 600 yards wide, and it immediately assumes that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, placid, and beautiful aspect which it maintains to its junction with the Mississippi. Its breadth varies exceedingly, being in some parts 1400 yards, whilst in others it is only 400 yards across. Between Pittsburg and its mouth it is diversified with about 100 considerable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, besides a great number of tow-heads (or barren sandy islands overgrown with willows) and sand-bars, which in low stages of the water greatly impede navigation. Some of these islands are of exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and afford most lovely situations for retired farms. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> among them, and the sandbars at their head, are great difficulties in the navigation of the river. Notwithstanding these obstacles, however, it is well adapted for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> navigation, the current being remarkably smooth and gentle, excepting at Louisville in Kentucky, where it is broken by falls, the water running for several miles with great rapidity, although not so much so as to be insurmountable by boats. A canal round these falls, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of great magnitude and utility, has been completed. The annual range of the Ohio, from low to high water, is about 50 feet; the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> range is 10 feet more. When lowest it may be forded at several places above Cincinnati. Throughout the year it is subject to sudden and very considerable elevations and depressions. Generally, the navigation is obstructed by floating <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a> for five or six weeks in winter. When the river is at its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> height, its current is about 3 miles an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>; when higher and rising it is more; and when very low it does not exceed 2 miles an hour. The Ohio and all its tributaries cannot, it is believed, have less than 5000 miles of waters navigable for boats; and taking all circumstances into account, few rivers in the world can vie with it, either in utility or beauty. From its very commencement it affords most delightful prospects. Rivers of a romantic and beautiful character flow into it almost at equal distances, like lateral canals. The aspect of the country on the banks has much <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, softness, and variety. Of the rivers and creeks which join it, the following are all navigable by steamboats for considerable distances, viz., the Muskingum, Great Kanawha, Big Sandy, Scioto, Miami, Kentucky, Green, Wabash, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TENNESSEE">Tennessee</a>. The last is by far the largest and most important tributary of the Ohio, watering considerable portions of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALABAMA">Alabama</a>, Tennessee, and Kentucky. Of creeks and smaller rivers there are probably nearly two hundred which enter the Ohio; but a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIST">list</a> of them would only be a dry catalogue of uncouth names. The area watered by the Ohio and its affluents is estimated at 200,000 square miles.

OHDRDRUF

Pages 500-500

a town of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha, in the principality of Gotha, on the Ohra, 8 miles S. of Gotha. It has a castle, a newly-erected town-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, and several churches and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a> of woollen cloth, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, organs, &c., are carried on here; and there are also numerous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> and bleach-works. The trade is considerable in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, coals, &c. Pop. 4559.

OHLAU

Pages 500-500
or OLAU, a town of Prussia, province of Silesia, government of Breslau, on the right bank of the Ohlau and left of the Oder, 18 miles S.E. of Breslau. It has a large castle, several churches, an orphan hospital, and a poor-house. There are extensive tobacco manufactories and a flour-mill, besides breweries, distilleries, &c. Pop. 6079.

OICH

Pages 500-505

LOCH, a lake of Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, between Loch Ness and Loch Lochy. It is about 4 miles in length by 1½ in breadth; it receives the Glengarry River, and discharges its waters by the Oich into Loch Ness. This loch is connected by the Caledonian Canal with Loch Ness and Loch Lochy. OILS. Under this head is ranged a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of organic compounds of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, both on account of their great economic value, and from the fact that they occur abundantly both in animals and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. They consist chiefly of carbon and hydrogen, but more <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> less of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a> is generally associated with them, and causes considerable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> in their qualities. They are either <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> or liquid, and in the former condition are more frequently termed fats. These fats are more abundant in the animal than in the vegetable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Oils, whether liquid or solid, usually consist of three other substances, two of which, stearine (or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>-suet), and margarine (adipose, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>), are solid; and the other, elaine or oleine, is liquid at ordinary temperatures. They are all from 6° to 9° <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and their liquid or solid condition depends upon the proportion in which their component parts are mixed. Thus, in the fats the oleine exists in small <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, and in the liquid oils it is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> constituent. A certain <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is necessary to the mixture, for at low temperatures there is a tendency to separation: the stearine and margarine are precipitated and solidified, and, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> pressed, can be entirely freed from the oleine. Both oils and fats, when boiled with water and alkali, undergo the peculiar <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of saponification, or, in other words, solidify, and become converted into soap; during this process a liquid of a sweet <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, called glycerine, is given off. (See GLYCERINE.) Glycerine exists in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and fats as a base to which stearic, margaric, and oleic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> are united, forming stearine, margarine, and oleine. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> uses to which oils and fats are applied are soap-making, illumination by candles or oil, lubricating machinery, and dressing cloth. They are easily separated by moderate pressure from the animal or vegetable tissues which contain them, but are not usually pure until they are rendered so by clarifying. Of the animal oils, those are chiefly solid which are fixed and yielded by the mammals and birds; whilst those derived volatilise from reptiles and fishes are for the most <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> liquid at the ordinary temperature. The true oils and fats are unchanged when heated even to a temperature above 400°; but there is another group of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> substances, termed essential oils, yielded by the vegetable kingdom, which are volatile at ordinary temperatures; hence the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> fixed oils is often applied to the former, and volatile oils to the latter. The volatility of the essential oils renders <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> a readily means of procuring many of them. They resemble the fixed oils in many respects, but differ materially in others; for instance, they do not undergo saponification when treated with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol4.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>; like them, however, they often separate at low temperatures into solid and liquid portions,—the former called steaopten, the latter elaopten. They are very slightly soluble in water, and they differ materially in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> they produce on the skin. Instead of the smooth soft feel of the true oils, they are harsh and rough to the touch. The essential oils are mostly pure hydro-carbons, but many are capable of absorbing oxygen when exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which darkens their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and renders them resinous in appearance, a result which may be seen generally around the mouths of bottles in which they are kept. Some are obtained already oxidized, and some are found to contain sulphur; hence they have been classified as pure hydro-carbons, when free from oxygen; oxidized essences, when obtained in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> with oxygen; and sulphuretted essences, when combined with sulphur. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> which the essential oils enter into render them peculiarly interesting to the student in organic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>. They appear to be the cause of all the more remarkable odours and flavours which characterize plants; and as they can generally be separated easily, they are very valuable in an economic point of view, affording us the means of concentrating and retaining the perfumes of the most evanescent <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, and in the same way of preserving the most pungent and delicate flavours. Essential oils are in some instances procured by simple pressure, as those from the rind of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> tribe; others are distilled with water, and float upon the condensed water in the receiver. Some, however, are so easily destroyed by these processes, that they can only be obtained by the power which the fixed oils have of absorbing them. Thus essence of jasmine is obtained by placing layers of the freshly-gathered flowers between layers of cotton-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> saturated with the fixed oil of almonds or of poppy seed, both of which are themselves odourless. They, however, soon absorb the essential oil naturally emitted from the flowers, and become highly perfumed. Fresh layers of flowers are supplied until the fixed oil is saturated, when it is pressed out from the cotton-wool. Besides the fixed oils and fats, and the essential oils, there is a mineral product called rock oil; it is not, however, properly speaking, an oil, but is a variety of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PETROLEUM">petroleum</a>, which exists abundantly in some bituminous shales. Works have been established in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a> and other parts of the kingdom for obtaining this material, but without much success. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">Large</a> quantities are, however, brought from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RANGOON">Rangoon</a>, in the Burmese empire, chiefly to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, where nearly 700 tons <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> were imported in 1857. Works exist at St Helen's, near Liverpool, and other places, where from this material, which is of a dark greenish-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> colour, and nearly the consistency of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>-coloured oil-like liquid is obtained, said to be very useful as a lubricant for machinery. A considerable proportion of paraffine is obtained from it, and it yields a very volatile naphtene. In enumerating the oils, those produced from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal kingdom</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> be first mentioned, and in the order of zoological classification; then the fixed vegetable oils; and finally the three classes of essential oils. Of the twelve orders into which naturalists divide the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a>, only four comprise animals which yield oils of economic value. These orders are Carnivora, Cetacea, Ruminantia, and Pachydermata. Of the carnivorous animals yielding oleaginous products, we have first the bear. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> bear (<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-URSUS">Ursus</a> Americanus, Gmelin), a native of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, yields an abundance of grease or soft fat; which is collected by the hunters who pursue the animal for its skin and hams, and is occasionally imported into this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, not, as some may suppose, to be used by the hairdressers and perfumers for pomades, but for the more useful manufacture of candles, &c. But the principal oil-producing carnivora are the seals, several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of which are killed on purpose. The quantity of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> oil imported is very great. Most of it comes from Newfoundland. The species which chiefly yield it are Callocephalus Groenlandicus, Callocephalus rituinus, Phoca barbata, and Arctocephalus Fulvifrons. The part which yields the oil in these animals is the blubber, a peculiar layer of oil-cells which lies immediately under the skin of the animal, and in fact constitutes a portion of the skin itself. Seal oil is liquid, and, when pure, of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PALE">pale</a> straw-colour. The first drawings from the blubber give the purest oil, which is obtained without pressure; but the succeeding drawings from the blubber-cask are more or less deeply coloured brown by the decomposition of the oil-cells. The Cetacea are remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of this peculiar skin-development called blubber, which in some species is one or two feet in thickness. This is not, however, the only source of the whale oil; for in the great-headed cachalot or sperm-whale (Cetodon macrocephalus, Cuv.), the gigantic head, which nearly equals the body in bulk, has an enormous receptacle on the upper part of the skull, from which oil is obtained. This receptacle consists of a dense bag divided into numerous large cells or compartments, in which the oil exists in a semi-fluid state, owing to the large quantity of stearine or spermaceti which it contains, and which can easily be separated from it by simple draining or slight pressure. The quantity of oil yielded by some of the larger whales, especially the cachalots, is enormous, but is often erroneously stated, owing to a misunderstanding of the fact that quantity in liquid oils is calculated by the ton <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, and not by the ton weight, as with solid oils or fats. A cachalot <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> yields 20 tons, or 5040 gallons; and single whales have been known to yield 30 tons (7680 gallons). The following oils derived from the whale tribe are known in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>—Sperm Oil, and its stearine, Spermaceti, from the cachalot; Trinita or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> Whale Oil, from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> Whale (Balaena mysticetus) and other species; Put-head Oil, from both Globicephalus deductor and Globicephalus Sinuatus; and Porpoise Oil, from Phocaena communis. These oils are usually imported as train or sperm oils; but the brokers are well skilled in distinguishing them. Of the ruminating animals, we have only two species which yield oleaginous products; but they are unequalled in value by any others. They are the ox (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BOS">Bos</a> taurus, Linn.), and the sheep (Ovis <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMON">ammon</a>, Linn.). The fat of both these animals melted <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> constitutes the tallow of commerce. They are so generally mixed together that there is no possibility of ascertaining the exact amount yielded by each. We receive our largest supply from Russia; but we import considerable quantities from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANSE">Hanse</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">Towns</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, South America (particularly Buenos Ayres and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTE_VIDEO">Monte Video</a>), the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, the East Indies, Australia, &c. That imported from the ports of Monte Video and Buenos Ayres is chiefly, if not altogether, ox tallow; whilst that from Australia is principally from the sheep. Besides the enormous quantity imported, we have to take into consideration that which is produced in Great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, which has been computed to be equal to the amount imported. From the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the feet of oxen a valuable oil is obtained. It contains comparatively little of the harder portion (stearine), and is in a fit state to be used for machinery. It is procured by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> the bones, and skimming off the fatty oil as it rises to the surface of the water. It is called neat's-foot oil; and from the fact that it remains liquid at a temperature below 32°, and is not liable to rancidity, it is peculiarly well adapted for turret clocks and other machinery much exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. The supply from such a source is necessarily limited. Of the Pachydermata only two yield oily products of any commercial importance. The first of these in point of value is the common <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a> (<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SUS">Sus</a> scrofa, Linn.), the fat of which, under the name of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>, is very extensively used. Considerable quantities are consumed in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of food. Most of the ointments of the pharmacist have lard for their base; and when too rancid for these purposes, it is used for greasing machinery, especially the axles of railway <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>. In the United States the production of lard is immense; and its stearine, which is easily separable from the lard, is extensively used in the manufacture of candles. The liquid stearine, under the name of lard oil, is used for the finer parts of machinery, and for that purpose is extensively imported into this country from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and America. The fat of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> does not, when melted, possess the same firm consistency as that of the ox, sheep, and swine. The proportion of stearine in it being comparatively small, it is only within the last eight years that it has attracted any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; but now it constitutes an important article of trade with Buenos Ayres and Monte Video, whence it is imported under the names of horse or mare's grease. The latter name is, however, more generally applied. From its liquidity, it is extremely penetrating; hence the ordinary packages for grease and tallow were found to be insufficient, as the casks were frequently half empty on their arrival. This checked its introduction for some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but it is now put into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> boxes lined with tin, and arrives without loss. It is found to answer very well as a lubricant for machinery. From the classes comprising the birds and the reptiles (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AVES">Aves</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REPTILIA">Reptilia</a>) neither oils nor fats of any importance are obtained, although the domesticated birds sometimes produce it in abundance. That of the goose, under the name of goose-grease, is occasionally heard of as a useful <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> remedy for various ailments. The class of fishes (Pisces) is a considerable source of oil, always of a clear liquid <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. It is nearly all yielded by one species, the common cod-fish (Gadus Morhua, Linn.). The Cod Oil, and the Cod-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> Oil of commerce, are both obtained from the liver of the fish; the latter, which is now so extensively used medicinally, being only prepared with a little more care. Its principal value as a remedial <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> appears to depend upon its nutritive qualities, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIGESTIVE">digestive</a> powers of a portion of pepsin, or biliary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, which is always present, and which may be detected by the application of a drop of concentrated sulphuric acid, when, if the oil be really cod-liver oil, a beautiful purple colour will be immediately produced. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cod-fish captured is incalculable. The cod-fishers, in opening the fishes to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and dry them, carefully preserve the livers, for which an extra <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> is usually in at- tendance; these are taken on shore, and piled up in immense masses exposed to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. The heat soon makes the oil run from the livers in considerable abundance, and for a short time it is very clear, and of a light straw colour,—this is the first quality, and is kept by itself. As the livers begin to decompose, however, they give a darker colour to the oil, and several qualities are obtained, the last of which is thick, turbid, and extremely offensive to the smell, and is known under the name of cod-pitchings. A small quantity of oil made from the common <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> (Clupea harengus, Linn.) is imported from time to time from North America; but its strong and unpleasant odour prevents it from being much used. The vegetable sources of oils are very numerous, and some are of great importance. **Fixed Vegetable Oils.**—Of these the most important is Olive Oil, procured from the ripe fruit of the olive (Olea Europaea, Linn.), which is cultivated for this purpose through all the countries of Southern Europe and Northern <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. Its native country is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. On Lebanon and the Mount of Olives, and in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>, the olive tree still grows wild. Its general <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> through the countries suitable to its growth is no doubt attributable to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, although the Carthaginians and others had previously procured and cultivated it. Pliny says (book xv., Bohn's edition), "Fenestella tells us that in the year of Rome 173, being the reign of Tarquinius Priscus, it did not exist in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, or Africa; whereas at the present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> it has crossed the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> even, and has been introduced into the provinces of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> and the middle of Spain. In the year of Rome 505, Appius Claudius, grandson of Appius Claudius Caecus, and L. Junius, being consuls, 12 pounds of oil sold for an as; and at a later <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, in the year 680, M. Seius, son of Lucius the curule edile, regulated the price of oil at Rome, at the rate of 10 pounds for the as, for the whole year. A person will be the less surprised at this, when he learns that twenty-two years after, in the third consulship of Cn. Pompeius, Italy was able to export oil to the provinces." Its value has never decreased; and, next to corn, olive oil is still perhaps the greatest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of the nations of Southern Europe. It has been described as the cream and butter of Spain and Italy; and the quantity consumed in those countries as food, entering into their cookery in every imaginable way, is immense. There are several varieties in cultivation, which vary much in quality. That which yields the sweet Italian and French salad oils is the var. s. longiflora, Aiton. Its fruit, when pickled unripe, is also most highly prized. The inferior oils of Spain are made from the large olive, var. s. latiflora, Aiton. In Italy and France the oil is obtained by crushing the fruit in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>,—the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of which are so set that they will thoroughly crush the pulpy part of the fruit without breaking the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or kernel in the centre. The fruit, which is gathered for the purpose when very ripe, is not unlike a small <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DAMSON">damson</a> in shape and colour, and the stone in the centre is very hard. After crushing in the mill, the pulp is put in bags made of rushes and slightly pressed, when the fine or virgin oil flows out abundantly. Afterwards the cake or marc is again broken up, mixed with water, and returned to the press, and an oil of an inferior quality is obtained. The cake or marc is once more broken up and mixed with water, after which it is placed in vats to ferment, and then again pressed. The result is an oil of a very inferior sort, only useful to the soap-makers. The oil of the olive is liquid at the ordinary temperature, but becomes solid a few degrees below 32°. In Spain the process is less carefully conducted.
